note: Questions that ask the child to draw. The answer should be a picture (drawn like our other pictures), not words. Work through this list when drawing resumes; the app shows the words under 'Your drawing should show' until a picture exists.

items.question: Draw the bag twice: when it was squeezed flat and twisted shut, and after you caught air in it.
items.answer_should_show: A flat, crinkly bag, and a fat, round bag.

items.question: Draw the air coming out of the bag onto your cheek. Show the moving air with lines.
items.answer_should_show: A bag near a face, with wavy lines going from the bag's neck to the cheek, and hair lifting.

items.question: Draw a glass full of chana. Use dots to show where the air is.
items.answer_should_show: A glass with round chana grains, and dots in all the gaps between the grains, right down to the bottom.

items.question: Draw a plant in a pot in the daytime and at night. Use arrows to show which gases go in and which come out.
items.answer_should_show: Day: carbon dioxide arrow going in, a big oxygen arrow coming out, and a small oxygen arrow going in. Night: only an oxygen arrow going in and a carbon dioxide arrow coming out.

items.question: Draw a zoom-in of the air inside a syringe before and after you push the plunger. Use dots for the particles.
items.answer_should_show: Before: a few dots spread far apart in a long space. After: the same number of dots, closer together, in a shorter space.

items.question: Draw a full glass upside down with a card under it. Draw one arrow for the push of the air and one for the push of the water. Make the arrows the right lengths.
items.answer_should_show: A glass upside down with a card. A long arrow pointing up on the card for the air. A very short arrow pointing down for the water.

items.question: Draw a straw standing in a glass of juice. Draw an arrow for the air pushing on the juice in the glass and another for the air pushing on the juice inside the straw while you sip. Which arrow is longer?
items.answer_should_show: A straw in a glass. A long arrow pointing down on the juice in the glass. A shorter arrow pointing down on the juice in the straw. The arrow in the glass is longer.

items.question: Draw a bottle of water with a small hole low down and the cap on tight, after the water has just stopped running. Draw arrows for the push of the air at the hole and for the air at the top of the water.
items.answer_should_show: A bottle with a hole low down. An arrow pointing in at the hole for the air outside. A smaller arrow on top of the water for the thinner air inside, with the water pushing out at the hole to balance.

items.question: Remember the la-la test, where you said only 'la-la' from behind a door. Draw the message slip that your listener guessed right most often.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing of one slip, for example the angry face with 'Go away!'.

items.question: Draw two birds. One sings a song on a rooftop at dawn. The other gives a short alarm call at a cat. Show how the two sounds are different.
items.answer_should_show: A bird with a long, wavy line of notes, and a bird with one short, sharp mark pointed at a cat.

items.question: Invent an animal who lives in a dark cave. Draw how they tell the others 'food is here!'. Will it be a sound, a touch or both? Write why.
items.answer_should_show: For example, a cave animal who clicks loudly and taps the ground, because in the dark nobody can see a body signal.

items.question: Draw a young chimpanzee learning to fish for termites. Show who she is watching and what tool she uses.
items.answer_should_show: A young chimpanzee next to her mother at a termite mound, both holding grass stems, the mother's stem covered in termites.

items.question: Draw the Pass It On chain as stick people in a row, with an arrow from each person to the next. Write the door each person used.
items.answer_should_show: A row of stick people with arrows, each labelled 'side door' or 'top door'.

items.question: Invent a new puzzle box for testing copying. Draw it, and label one useless step and the step that really opens it.
items.answer_should_show: Any clear drawing with one labelled useless step, such as a button that does nothing, and one real way in.

items.question: Draw a line graph of a volunteer's jumps for 12 spoon rings, then one rice-tin shake, then one more spoon ring.
items.answer_should_show: A line that starts high, around 2, falls to near 0 by ring 8 to 12, jumps up at the rice tin, and then falls to 0 at the last spoon ring.

items.question: A bee gets nectar from 6 of the first 8 flowers. The paying colour then changes, and she gets nectar from 2 of the next 8. She then gets nectar from 6 of the last 8. Draw a line graph with three points.
items.answer_should_show: A line that starts at 6, dips to 2, and rises back to 6.

items.question: Draw a model of two nerve cells before and after many gentle touches. Show what changes at the gap.
items.answer_should_show: Two cells with a gap. Before: many chemical dots cross the gap. After: fewer dots cross the gap.

items.question: Draw an ant nest cut open. Show the queen, eggs, young workers caring for the eggs, and older workers going out.
items.answer_should_show: A nest with a queen deep inside, eggs near her, young workers next to the eggs, and older workers near the entrance and outside.

items.question: Draw a graph of your sugar drop test: minutes along the bottom, number of ants up the side, with one line for each drop.
items.answer_should_show: Two lines, both starting near zero. The strong-drop line rises faster and higher. The weak-drop line stays low.

items.question: Draw a cartoon strip in four boxes showing how an elephant calf learns the way to the river from her grandmother, and later shows her own calf.
items.answer_should_show: Box 1: calf walks behind grandmother in a dry year. Box 2: they reach the river. Box 3: years later, the calf is grown and leading. Box 4: she leads her own calf to the river.

items.question: Draw the door of a beehive and three bees at it. Show a guard, a bee that is fanning her wings, and a forager coming home with pollen. Write one label for each.
items.answer_should_show: A hive door with three bees. The guard stands at the door facing a bee that has just arrived. The fanning bee has her wings blurred, and she stands at the entrance. The forager has yellow lumps on her back legs.

items.question: Draw two bee dances on the comb. One is for flowers close to the hive, and one is for flowers very far away. Show what is different.
items.answer_should_show: Two combs. On the first, a short waggle run. On the second, a much longer waggle run. Both runs lean at some angle from straight up.

items.question: Draw a termite mound cut in half. Show the queen's chamber, a fungus garden, and a tunnel with a soldier in it.
items.answer_should_show: A mound shape with tunnels. In the middle, a chamber with a large queen. Beside it, a garden of small round balls with a fungus on them. In one tunnel, a soldier with a large head.

items.question: Remember the stop test. Draw your leg three times: relaxed, trying to stop, and pulling your fingers. Show how big each kick was with an arrow.
items.answer_should_show: Three legs. Usually a long arrow for relaxed, a shorter arrow or none for trying to stop, and the longest arrow for pulling.

items.question: Draw a round spider web, the kind many spiders spin at dusk. Show the spokes and the spiral.
items.answer_should_show: A web with lines going out from the middle like the spokes of a wheel, and a spiral going round and round across the spokes.

items.question: Draw a cartoon in two boxes. Box 1: something you could do as a newborn baby. Box 2: something you learned this year.
items.answer_should_show: Box 1 might show a baby gripping, crying or drinking milk. Box 2 might show reading, swimming or cycling.

items.question: Draw a moth on a tree trunk, coloured so that a bird would find her hard to see. Then draw the same moth on a white wall.
items.answer_should_show: Two drawings: a moth with bark-like colours and lines on a tree trunk, and the same moth standing out on a white wall.

items.question: Draw an antlion's pit from the side. Show where the antlion waits, and how an ant slides in.
items.answer_should_show: A cone-shaped pit with sloping sides, the antlion buried at the bottom with jaws showing, and an ant slipping down one side.

items.question: Invent an animal who lives on your bedroom floor or bedsheet. Draw them with camouflage for that place, and write how they find their food.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing of an invented animal coloured to match the chosen floor or sheet, with a sentence on how they get food, such as waiting in ambush for crumbs or ants.

items.question: Draw the floor from above in your bowl test. Show the bowl, the usual start and the secret start. Draw a dot where you stopped from each start.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with the bowl at one end, two starts side by side, and dots: one near the bowl from the usual start, one off to the side from the secret start.

items.question: Draw a bird before and after getting ready for a long flight. Show where she stores her fuel.
items.answer_should_show: Two birds: a thin one, and a rounder one with fat under the skin of the belly and chest.

items.question: Design a city building that is safer for birds that fly at night. Draw it and label two features.
items.answer_should_show: A building with lights that are off or shaded at night, glass with patterns birds can see, or no lights pointing up at the sky.

items.question: Draw a graph line for a bird that rests at a lake for 3 weeks, flies south for 1 week, then rests at another lake for 3 weeks.
items.answer_should_show: A line that is flat for 3 weeks, drops steeply for 1 week, then is flat again for 3 weeks.

items.question: Draw a chain from the Sun to a swallow catching an insect. Mark one place where the chain could break.
items.answer_should_show: A line from the Sun to plants, to insects, to the swallow, with a mark such as a drained pond or sprayed field where the chain could break.

items.question: Draw yourself as a baby, and yourself now. Make the baby's head the right size for the baby's body.
items.answer_should_show: A baby with a big head, about a quarter of the body, and short legs. A child now with a smaller head for the body, and longer legs.

items.question: Here is a silkworm, eating a mulberry leaf. Draw what the silkworm will grow into.
items.answer_should_show: A moth with wings: the silk moth.

items.question: Paper chick mouths of four colours, including yellow and black, are laid on a dark cloth in dim light. Draw them, and show which colour you think gets found most.
items.answer_should_show: A dark nest with paper circles, and most chana on the yellow ones.

items.question: Draw yourself as a baby, doing one thing that helped someone look after you.
items.answer_should_show: A baby crying, gripping a finger, smiling or reaching up.

items.question: Design a nest for chicks in a dark hole. Draw the chicks with mouths that are easy for the parents to find.
items.answer_should_show: A dark hole with chicks whose mouths have bright, light edges.

items.question: Pick a food: seeds, fish or nectar. Draw the head of a bird with a beak that fits that food.
items.answer_should_show: A bird head with a short, thick beak for seeds, a long, straight, sharp beak for fish, or a long, thin, curved beak for nectar.

items.question: Look at the card 'One bone plan in many limbs'. Draw your arm and a bat's wing side by side. Colour the same bones the same colour.
items.answer_should_show: An arm and a bat wing, each with one long upper bone, two lower bones, small wrist bones and long finger bones in the wing.

items.question: Draw a fish. Draw arrows to show where water goes in and where it goes out. Colour the gills.
items.answer_should_show: An arrow into the mouth, an arrow out from under the gill cover, and red gills under the cover.

items.question: Draw a bat hunting a moth at night. Draw lines to show the bat's sounds going out and the echo coming back.
items.answer_should_show: A bat, a moth, curved lines going from the bat to the moth, and curved lines coming back to the bat's ears.

items.question: Draw the outline of a child's upper body. Draw the breathing system inside it and label four parts: nose, windpipe, lungs, diaphragm.
items.answer_should_show: The nose and windpipe at the top, two lungs in the chest, and the diaphragm as a dome of muscle under the lungs, each with a label.

items.question: Draw one camel with fat spread all over her body, and one camel with her fat in a hump. Draw arrows for heat leaving each one.
items.answer_should_show: Two camels. The first has a thick layer all around with few or no arrows. The second has a hump on her back and arrows leaving her bare sides.

items.question: Draw an octopus squeezing into a crack in a rock. Label the one big hard part that sets how small a gap she can pass.
items.answer_should_show: An octopus with soft arms and body flowing into a crack, and a label pointing to the beak between her arms.

items.question: Draw an octopus using her jet. Show the water going out backwards and the octopus going forward. Add arrows.
items.answer_should_show: An octopus with a funnel pointing backwards, an arrow for the water going back and an arrow for the octopus going forward.

items.question: Draw the life cycle of a hen as a circle, with arrows between the stages. Then write one way it is different from a frog's life cycle.
items.answer_should_show: Egg, chick, adult hen, with an arrow back to the egg. A strong answer says the chick already looks like a small hen, while a tadpole looks nothing like a frog.

items.question: Draw the life cycle of a grasshopper and of a butterfly side by side. Circle the stage that the grasshopper does not have.
items.answer_should_show: Grasshopper: egg, nymph, adult. Butterfly: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. The chrysalis, or pupa, is circled.

items.question: Draw a waiting group of cells inside a caterpillar. Then draw what they become inside the chrysalis.
items.answer_should_show: A tiny flat patch of cells inside the caterpillar, then a big wing inside the chrysalis.

items.question: Draw a frog's life cycle as a circle with four pictures. Label each picture.
items.answer_should_show: A circle with arrows: jelly eggs in water, a tadpole, a young frog with legs, an adult frog on land.

items.question: Draw one ready-born and one helpless-born newborn side by side. Show one thing that tells them apart.
items.answer_should_show: For example, a calf standing next to a blind kitten, or a hen's chick pecking next to a naked sparrow chick.

items.question: Draw a bar chart for four animals' lifespans: mouse 2 years, dog 12 years, elephant 60 years and human 75 years. Label the bars.
items.answer_should_show: Four bars with heights in the ratio 2 to 12 to 60 to 75, labelled with the animals' names and years.

items.question: Draw a crow using a tool. Label the tool and what the crow wants to get.
items.answer_should_show: A crow holding a twig or wire hook in their beak, reaching into a hole or tube, with a grub or food labelled.

items.question: Draw what you think is happening inside a crow's brain as they bend a wire. Show neurons passing a signal.
items.answer_should_show: A crow's head with many tiny neurons joined by lines, with sparks or arrows moving along them.

items.question: Draw 8 dots in two ways: one way that is quick to know at a glance, and one way that is hard. Write why.
items.answer_should_show: Eight dots as two groups of four in neat rows, and eight dots scattered. The groups are quick because you see two small groups.

items.question: Draw a simple picture of the ratio effect. Show a pair of dot groups that is easy to tell apart and a pair that is hard.
items.answer_should_show: An easy pair such as 4 and 8 dots, and a hard pair such as 8 and 9 dots, labelled easy and hard.

items.question: Design a quick test for a street dog, who has no number words. Draw the two plates, and write what you would control.
items.answer_should_show: Two plates with different numbers of biscuit pieces, with a coin for sides. Controls: the size of the pieces, the smell, the side and a helper who does not know the answer.

items.question: Draw your mouth, open wide. Colour the front teeth that bite red. Colour the back teeth that chew blue.
items.answer_should_show: Thin front teeth coloured red, wide back teeth coloured blue.

items.question: Draw a bird's footprints for walking, and a bird's footprints for hopping.
items.answer_should_show: Walking: one-two-one-two, one foot ahead of the other. Hopping: two footprints side by side, in pairs.

items.question: Draw a dough animal that could stand up by itself. Show how many legs it needs and where they go.
items.answer_should_show: A dough body on three or more legs, spread out.

items.question: Draw an animal you saw today. Colour their covering carefully.
items.answer_should_show: Any real animal, with their covering drawn: feathers, fur, scales, a shell or bare skin.

items.question: Draw a fish with all their fins. Draw an arrow on the fin that pushes the fish forward.
items.answer_should_show: A fish with a tail fin, a back fin and side fins, and an arrow on the tail fin.

items.question: Invent an animal that lives on a steep rock wall. Draw their feet, and show how they hold on.
items.answer_should_show: A made-up animal with feet that grip, such as sticky toes, hooks or many legs.

items.question: Draw one animal home you have seen near your house. Label who lives there and what the home is made of.
items.answer_should_show: Any real home, with labels. For example, a crow's nest of sticks and wire in a tree, a web on a gate, or an anthill by a wall.

items.question: Draw a timeline of one animal's day, from sunrise to night. Use what you saw in My Animal Week.
items.answer_should_show: A line from sunrise to night, with drawings of what the animal did at each time. For example, a crow calling at dawn, feeding in the morning, resting at noon and flying to the roost at sunset.

items.question: Draw a bird. Colour the feathers. Show the beak, two wings and two legs.
items.answer_should_show: A bird with feathers, a beak, two wings and two legs.

items.question: Draw the three cups from your bean test. Draw the beans from each cup in a line underneath.
items.answer_should_show: Three lines of beans of different lengths, labelled morning, afternoon and evening.

items.question: Draw a pigeon on a cold morning and a pigeon on a hot afternoon.
items.answer_should_show: A round, fluffed-up pigeon for the cold morning, and a thin, sleek pigeon for the hot afternoon.

items.question: Remember the crumb test. Draw the four sizes of crumb on the paper, and draw what the ants did with each size.
items.answer_should_show: Four sizes of crumb. Ants carrying the tiny ones, a team pulling a rice-sized one, and many ants crowded on the big ones.

items.question: Draw a spider and an insect side by side. Show the right number of legs and body parts on each.
items.answer_should_show: An insect with three body parts, six legs on the middle part and two antennae. A spider with two body parts, eight legs on the front part and no antennae.

items.question: Draw how an earthworm moves, in three pictures: long and thin, then short and fat, then long and thin again, further along.
items.answer_should_show: Three drawings of a worm. In the second, the body is short and fat. In the third, the front end has moved further forward.

items.question: Draw an ant. Show their 3 body parts and 6 legs. Label the head.
items.answer_should_show: A head with two feelers, a middle part with all 6 legs attached, and a back end.

items.question: Draw a starfish from underneath. Show their mouth and the tube feet on each arm.
items.answer_should_show: Five arms around a middle, a mouth in the centre, and rows of small dots or bubbles along each arm for tube feet.

items.question: Draw a simple family tree with these animals on the branches: jellyfish, snail, ant, starfish, fish, you. Put the closest cousins next to each other.
items.answer_should_show: Jellyfish on an early low branch. Then a split: snail and ant on one side, starfish, fish and you on the other side, with starfish branching off just before fish and you.

items.question: Draw an ant. Show where the air goes in and how it reaches her legs.
items.answer_should_show: An ant with holes along her sides, thick tubes running inward, and fine branches reaching the head, tummy and legs.

items.question: Draw a spider from below. Show a book lung as a stack of thin plates, and label the air opening.
items.answer_should_show: A spider's belly with a small slit, and a stack of thin plates like pages inside it.

items.question: Draw two bodies, one thin and one thick. Show with arrows how oxygen can reach the middle of each.
items.answer_should_show: A thin body with short arrows through the skin, and a thick body with branching tubes, folds or a pump bringing the air inside.

items.question: Remember the Bendy Backbone test. Draw the whole straw and the 8-piece chain wrapped round the tumbler.
items.answer_should_show: A straight straw touching the tumbler at one point, and a chain of 8 pieces curving close round the tumbler.

items.question: Make up a new reptile and draw them. Show two clues that tell people your animal is a reptile.
items.answer_should_show: A made-up animal with dry scales, and eggs with shells laid on land, or lungs.

items.question: In the Bendy Backbone test you tried 1, 2, 4 and 8 pieces. Predict and draw what a chain of 16 pieces would look like round the tumbler.
items.answer_should_show: An almost perfect circle round the tumbler, with almost no gaps.

items.question: Draw a fish. Draw arrows to show water going in at the mouth, over the gills and out at the side.
items.answer_should_show: Arrows go in at the mouth, over the gills behind the eye, and out under the gill flap.

items.question: Draw a bird's egg, cut in half. Show the shell, the baby, the yolk for food, and the tiny holes that let air in.
items.answer_should_show: A shell with dots for holes, a small curled chick, a yellow yolk, and clear watery white around them.

items.question: A mother bird sits on her eggs on a cold, windy night. Draw her from the side, cut in half. Label how her body heat reaches the eggs, and what stops the heat escaping.
items.answer_should_show: The mother's belly touching the eggs, with a bare patch of skin there, labelled 'her heat goes into the eggs'. Fluffed feathers around her and the nest under the eggs, labelled 'trapped still air keeps the heat in'.

items.question: Draw a pond as a fish would sense it. Show where the lateral line is, and draw arrows for the ripples it feels.
items.answer_should_show: A fish with a line along her side, and ripple lines reaching that line from an insect on the surface.

items.question: Draw a top view of a pigeon and an owl. Shade how far round each one can see, and write the angle beside each shape.
items.answer_should_show: A pigeon with a very wide shaded wedge of about 340 degrees, and an owl with a narrow wedge of about 110 degrees with a larger overlap in front.

items.question: Draw an owl's face from the front. Add arrows to show how the face works as a dish that gathers sound.
items.answer_should_show: A heart-shaped face with arrows curving inwards from the sides towards the ears.

items.question: Draw your hand. Draw one basic need on each finger.
items.answer_should_show: Air, water, food, clothes and a home, one on each finger.

items.question: Draw the fan and the tissue flag. Draw lines to show the moving air.
items.answer_should_show: The flag points away from the fan, with lines of air between them.

items.question: Draw a home for a pigeon. Show what keeps off the rain and the wind.
items.answer_should_show: A nest on a ledge under a roof, or in a corner with a wall on the windy side.

items.question: Draw a room in a flat from above, with two windows on opposite sides. Draw arrows to show how fresh air comes in and used air goes out.
items.answer_should_show: A square room with a window on each side. Arrows come in through one window, cross the room and go out through the other.

items.question: Draw how water leaves your body during one day. Show at least three ways.
items.answer_should_show: A child with arrows showing water leaving as breath from the mouth and nose, as sweat or unseen water from the skin, and as urine. A strong drawing may also show tears.

items.question: Design an ant-proof stand for a jar of jaggery. Draw it and label the part that stops the ants.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing of a jar on a small stand, with the stand's legs in bowls of water, or the jar on an island in a plate of water. The water is labelled as the part that stops the ants. A strong design makes sure nothing touches the jar from outside.

items.question: Draw your hand picking up a grain of rice. Colour the thumb red.
items.answer_should_show: A hand with the thumb and first finger pressing together, a small grain between them, and the thumb coloured red.

items.question: Your thumb is taped down. Draw a tool you could make to pick up a bean.
items.answer_should_show: Any tool that holds the bean from two sides, like tongs, a clothes peg or two sticks, or one that scoops, like a spoon.

items.question: Draw your hand. Mark the places people most often forget when washing.
items.answer_should_show: Thumbs, fingertips and nails, between the fingers, and the backs of the hands.

items.question: Draw yourself after running on a hot day. Show where the sweat comes out of your skin. Draw arrows to show what happens to your body's heat as the sweat dries.
items.answer_should_show: Drops of sweat on the forehead, face and arms, coming out of tiny holes called pores. Arrows show heat leaving the skin as the sweat dries into the air.

items.question: Design a new guard for one body part. Label what it does and how it works.
items.answer_should_show: Any creative design with a clear job. For example: ear flaps that close in loud places, like a hippo's ears closing under water.

items.question: Draw the same person at three ages: 5, 35 and 75. Show and label at least three body changes.
items.answer_should_show: A small child with a big head and milk teeth. A tall adult. An older person with grey hair, some wrinkles and reading glasses.

items.question: Draw two eyes from the side. Give one a soft, round lens for a child. Give the other a flatter, stiffer lens for an elder. Draw a book close to each eye. Label each book sharp or blurry.
items.answer_should_show: The child's round lens makes the close book sharp. The elder's stiff lens makes the close book blurry.

items.question: Design a bus stop sign that an elder with a stiff eye lens can read from the bench. Label two choices you made, and which body change each one helps with.
items.answer_should_show: For example: big, dark letters on a light background, for older eyes. A picture of the bus number, so it can be read from far away. A loud and flashing light when the bus comes, for ears that hear less.

items.question: Draw a graph of a person's height from birth to age 90. Show where it rises fast, where it stops, and where it drops a little in old age.
items.answer_should_show: A steep rise in the first year, a slower rise in childhood, a fast rise in the teenage growth spurt, then flat from the late teens. Near the end it dips a little, because the spine gets a little shorter in old age.

items.question: Remember the bedtime and morning test. Draw the paper strip with your blue bedtime line and your red morning line.
items.answer_should_show: A strip with a red line a little above the blue line, with names.

items.question: Draw yourself in clothes from three years ago. Show with arrows where they are too small.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with arrows at the wrists, knees or waist.

items.question: Draw two backbones: one in the evening, after a long day, and one in the morning, after sleep.
items.answer_should_show: Evening: thin, flat discs. Morning: thicker, rounder discs.

items.question: Draw a picture graph of how tall a person is at 0, 1, 7, 15 and 30 years old.
items.answer_should_show: Five people getting taller quickly at first, then more slowly, with the 15-year-old and 30-year-old close in height.

items.question: Draw a heart in the middle of a body outline. Draw red arrows to show blood going out to the head, the arms and the legs, and coming back.
items.answer_should_show: Arrows go out from the heart to the head, arms and legs, and other arrows come back to the heart, making loops.

items.question: Draw the figure of eight of blood. Put the heart in the middle, the lungs on the top loop, and the body on the bottom loop. Colour blood bright red after the lungs and darker red after the body.
items.answer_should_show: A figure of eight with the heart in the middle. Bright red goes from the lungs to the heart and out to the body. Darker red comes back from the body to the heart and on to the lungs.

items.question: Draw the heart as two pumps side by side. Show an arrow from the right pump to the lungs, and an arrow from the left pump to the body, and one arrow back to each.
items.answer_should_show: Two pumps side by side. An arrow goes from the right one to the lungs and back to the left one. An arrow goes from the left one to the body and back to the right one.

items.question: A child's pulse after exercise was 138 at 0 minutes, 112 at 1 minute, 98 at 2 minutes, 90 at 3 minutes and 86 at 4 minutes. Draw a line graph of these.
items.answer_should_show: A graph with minutes along the bottom from 0 to 4 and pulse up the side. The line starts high at 138 and drops steeply, then flattens out near 86.

items.question: Draw a baby in the womb. Label the womb, the water, the cord and the placenta.
items.answer_should_show: A curled baby inside a round womb, with water all round them, and a cord from the baby's tummy to a round placenta on the womb wall.

items.question: Draw a line on a long strip of paper from 0 weeks to 40 weeks. Mark where the heart starts to beat, where fingers form, where hearing starts, and birth.
items.answer_should_show: A line with marks at about 6 weeks for the heart, about 12 weeks for fingers, about 24 weeks for hearing, and 40 weeks for birth.

items.question: Design a carrier that keeps a raw egg safe on the stairs. Label two features that copy how the womb protects a baby.
items.answer_should_show: Good features: water or soft padding all round the egg, a soft inner layer like the womb wall, and a snug fit so the egg cannot bang about.

items.question: Draw three stages of a hand forming: a flat paddle, a paddle with finger lines, and five separate fingers. Mark the cells that die.
items.answer_should_show: Three small drawings in order: a flat paddle shape, a paddle with faint lines, five fingers. The gaps between the lines are marked or shaded.

items.question: Draw a row of six cells with a signal source at the left end. Shade each cell to show how much signal reaches that cell, and label three different jobs.
items.answer_should_show: Six cells in a row, the leftmost darkest and the rightmost palest, with three labels such as 'job A' near the source, 'job B' in the middle and 'job C' far from it.

items.question: Draw the placenta as a model: two bloodstreams close together with a thin wall between them. Use arrows to show oxygen and waste.
items.answer_should_show: Two channels side by side, one labelled mother's blood and one labelled baby's blood, with a thin line between. An arrow for oxygen goes from the mother's side to the baby's. An arrow for waste goes the other way.

items.question: Draw a scraped knee as if it were cut in half, seen from the side. Show the skin, a blood vessel, white blood cells, pus and a scab. Label each one.
items.answer_should_show: A side view with the skin on top and a gap where it was scraped. A blood vessel runs below. White blood cells are coming out of the vessel towards the gap. Pus sits in the gap, and a scab covers the top.

items.question: Draw three pictures to show a phagocyte eating a germ: touch, wrap, swallow.
items.answer_should_show: 1. A blob cell touching a small germ. 2. The cell's edges wrapping around the germ. 3. The germ inside the cell.

items.question: Draw the body's defences as a castle, with walls, gates, guards and a heat knob. Label each one with the body part it stands for.
items.answer_should_show: A castle with a skin wall, eye, nose and mouth gates with tears, mucus and saliva, white blood cell guards on a blood road, and a heat knob for fever, all labelled.

items.question: Draw an antibody holding on to the spike of a germ. Show how the shapes fit.
items.answer_should_show: A Y-shaped antibody with one tip fitting into a notch or a spike on a round germ.

items.question: Draw a graph with two lines. One shows antibodies during a first infection. The other shows antibodies during a second infection with the same germ.
items.answer_should_show: The first line rises slowly over about a week or more to a low peak. The second line rises in two to four days to a much higher peak.

items.question: Draw a town where most houses have a shield and a few do not. Show the germ's path stopping at the shields.
items.answer_should_show: A grid of houses, most with shield marks, a few without, and arrows showing the germ spreading from one sick house and stopping at the shields.

items.question: Draw yourself on a hot day and on a cold day. Label two things your body does in each.
items.answer_should_show: Hot: sweat, red cheeks. Cold: shivering, goosebumps or pale fingers.

items.question: Draw a feedback loop for being too cold. Use three arrows: notice, decide, act.
items.answer_should_show: Skin sensors notice the cold. The hypothalamus decides. Muscles shiver and skin makes goosebumps. Then the body checks again.

items.question: Draw the Earth's slow rock thermostat as a loop: Earth gets warmer, more rain and weathering, less carbon dioxide in the air, Earth cools.
items.answer_should_show: A loop of four arrows: warmer Earth, more rain washing rocks, less carbon dioxide, cooler Earth, back to the start.

items.question: Draw a see-saw. Write insulin at one end and glucagon at the other. Draw a small ball near the middle for the sugar level.
items.answer_should_show: A see-saw with insulin labelled on the end pushing down, glucagon on the other end pushing up, and a ball near the middle.

items.question: Draw a graph of pulse against time, from rest, through a run, to recovery. Mark the steepest part of the recovery.
items.answer_should_show: A line that starts low, rises steeply during the run, falls steeply in the first minute after, then falls more slowly back to the starting level. The steepest fall is just after stopping.

items.question: Draw the Level Bottle when the level is steady. Draw an arrow for the water going in, an arrow for the water going out, and show how long each one is.
items.answer_should_show: A bottle with a hole near the base, a trickle entering at the top, an arrow in and an arrow out, both the same length.

items.question: Draw the rib cage around a heart and two lungs. Show the gaps between the ribs.
items.answer_should_show: Curved ribs like the bars of a cage, a heart in the middle tipped left, two lungs filling the rest, and small gaps between the ribs.

items.question: Draw one cell. Inside, draw a mitochondrion, the part that uses oxygen, and a small bag of juice that breaks down food. On the outside, draw a few sensors. Write what each one does.
items.answer_should_show: A round cell with a small bean shape (uses oxygen to make energy), a small bubble (breaks down food and old bits) and little feelers on the outside (sense chemicals around the cell).

items.question: Draw the shape of a pulse rising when exercise starts and falling when it stops. Mark with an arrow where it changes fastest.
items.answer_should_show: A line that rises steeply at the start and then flattens, and then falls steeply after stopping and flattens again. The arrows point to the steepest parts.

items.question: Draw a side view of a chest breathing in and breathing out. Show the diaphragm and the ribs in both pictures.
items.answer_should_show: Two pictures. Breathing in: the diaphragm is flat and the ribs are lifted. Breathing out: the diaphragm is domed upwards and the ribs are lower.

items.question: Draw a diagram of the two routes that control your breathing. Use arrows to show the automatic route from the brainstem and the take-over route from the thinking part of the brain.
items.answer_should_show: A brain with two arrows. One arrow goes from the brainstem to the breathing muscles, marked automatic. A second arrow goes from the top of the brain to the same muscles, marked I decide.

items.question: Remember the Bend and Dot activity. Draw one of your fingers. Put a dot at every place it bends.
items.answer_should_show: A finger with three dots: at the big knuckle, the middle and near the tip.

items.question: In the torch test, what did the light do when you moved only your elbow? Draw it on the wall.
items.answer_should_show: A straight or curved line going up and down, not a circle.

items.question: Remember the Muscle Feel activity. Draw your upper arm muscle when your arm is straight, and when you lift the bottle.
items.answer_should_show: A long thin muscle when the arm is straight, and a short fat bump when the arm is bent.

items.question: Design a robot arm that must stir a pot of sambar round and round. Draw it, and mark which joints are hinges and which are balls.
items.answer_should_show: An arm with at least one ball and socket joint or a turning joint, so the spoon can go round.

items.question: Draw the glass of vinegar with the eggshell in it, just after you dropped the shell in.
items.answer_should_show: A glass of liquid with a piece of shell, and small bubbles on the shell and rising up.

items.question: Draw the two pencils in the dough from the root test. Show how deep each one went.
items.answer_should_show: A block of dough with one pencil deep in it and one only a little way in.

items.question: Design a toothbrush that makes it easy to clean the very back molars. Draw it, and label one thing that makes it good.
items.answer_should_show: Any design with a reason, such as a small head, a bent neck or soft bristles.

items.question: Draw a candle burning. Add arrows to show the melted wax climbing the wick and turning into gas at the flame.
items.answer_should_show: A candle with a pool of melted wax at the top, an arrow going up the wick, and a label 'wax gas' just under the flame.

items.question: Draw the fire triangle. Write fuel, oxygen and heat on its sides. Then draw one way to take away each side.
items.answer_should_show: A triangle labelled fuel, oxygen and heat, with, for example, a gas regulator turned off by fuel, a lid by oxygen, and water by heat.

items.question: In the Tea Strainer Test, the fine mesh stopped the flame. Draw what you saw from the side: the candle, the flame and the mesh. Show where the smoke went.
items.answer_should_show: A candle, a flame flattened under the mesh, and smoke rising above the mesh.

items.question: Design a lamp for a coal mine, using what you learned about metal mesh. Label the flame, the mesh, and where air comes in.
items.answer_should_show: A flame inside a cylinder of fine metal mesh, with air coming in through the mesh and a solid top or shield.

items.question: Draw a timeline from early people keeping fire to you lighting a gas stove. Put at least four steps on it.
items.answer_should_show: For example: keeping fires from wildfires, carrying embers, making fire with a fire drill, oil lamps, matches, gas stoves.

items.question: Draw a candle with a cold plate above it. Draw arrows to show where the water and the soot collect, and label them.
items.answer_should_show: A candle flame with a plate above it, an arrow to drops of water on the plate's underside, and an arrow to a black patch of soot.

items.question: Draw the steel wool balance at three moments: before burning, while it burns, and after it has cooled. Show which side is lower each time.
items.answer_should_show: Three drawings of a skewer hung from its middle. Before: level. While burning: level or nearly. After cooling: the burnt side lower.

items.question: Draw wax atoms and oxygen atoms before burning, and carbon dioxide and water after burning. Use circles for atoms and show that none are lost.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with carbon, hydrogen and oxygen circles joined in groups on the left. On the right, the same circles in new groups, carbon dioxide and water, with the same number of each kind of circle.

items.question: Draw the katori of melted butter before the freezer, and after.
items.answer_should_show: A runny yellow puddle, then a solid pale yellow layer.

items.question: Draw what you think happens inside one rice grain when it is boiled. Show where the water goes.
items.answer_should_show: A grain with water drops going into it and the inside swelling.

items.question: Draw the frozen piece of dough when it came out of the freezer, and again after you held it in your warm hands.
items.answer_should_show: A flat, stiff disc, perhaps with frost on it, then a soft ball or a soft bent disc.

items.question: Draw a change that cannot be undone that you have seen in your kitchen. Draw it before and after, with an arrow between.
items.answer_should_show: For example, white rice grains, then soft cooked rice, or raw batter, then a dosa.

items.question: Most green sketch pens are a mixture of two dyes. Draw what a green dot might look like after the water has climbed the strip. Colour and label each band.
items.answer_should_show: A strip with a pencil line at the bottom, a band of one colour, such as blue, and a band of another colour, such as yellow, above or below it.

items.question: Draw the flame in the flame test for each of the three cups: plain water, sugar water and salt water. Colour each flame and label it.
items.answer_should_show: Three flames: a blue flame for plain water, perhaps with a tiny orange spark, a blue flame for sugar water, and a bright yellow-orange flame for salt water.

items.question: Predict: you put a yellow dot and a blue dot on top of each other on one strip, and run it. Draw what you expect. Then draw what a green sketch pen strip looked like, if you tested one. Are they alike?
items.answer_should_show: Two strips. The yellow and blue mix splits into a yellow band and a blue band. The green strip may show the same two colours.

items.question: Draw three glasses of cabbage water: one with lemon juice, one with plain water and one with soapy water. Colour each glass the colour you saw, and label it acid, neutral or base.
items.answer_should_show: Lemon glass pink, labelled acid. Plain water glass purple, labelled neutral. Soapy water glass blue-green, labelled base.

items.question: Draw a long strip for the colour line. Colour it from pink at one end to green at the other. Put these on it in the right place: lemon, buttermilk, water, soda water, detergent water.
items.answer_should_show: Pink end: lemon, then buttermilk a little towards the middle. Purple middle: water. Then soda water in the blue part, and detergent water in the green part near the end.

items.question: Draw what you think is happening, too small to see, when an acid and a base meet in water. Use one shape for the acid's hydrogen particles and another shape for the base's particles.
items.answer_should_show: Two kinds of shapes moving about, then pairs joining into new shapes labelled water. Fewer free acid and base particles are left.

items.question: Draw a slice of the stomach wall with its three defences: the acid in the middle, a coat of mucus and the wall with new cells.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with acid at the top, a thick layer of mucus in the middle with bubbles of bicarbonate, and a wall of cells at the bottom, some of them marked new.

items.question: Draw a dye ladder of five cups that shows how the colour fades when every step is ten times weaker.
items.answer_should_show: Five cups in a row, each with a colour much paler than the one before, with a label such as 1 in 10, 1 in 100, 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 10,000 under them.

items.question: Draw the stomach as an acid room, the small intestine as a near-neutral room and the bicarbonate that comes between them.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with a strongly coloured stomach, a pale intestine, and an arrow from the pancreas carrying bicarbonate into the start of the intestine.

items.question: Draw a water molecule. Use a big circle for oxygen and small circles for hydrogen. Draw a line for each bond. Label each atom.
items.answer_should_show: A big circle labelled O, with two small circles labelled H, each joined to the O by one line.

items.question: Draw carbon dioxide, CO2. Carbon is in the middle and an oxygen is on each side. Draw a line for every bond, so every atom uses all its hands.
items.answer_should_show: O, C, O in a row, with two lines between the carbon and each oxygen.

items.question: Draw a box of ice and a box of steam. Show the water molecules in each. Do the molecules change, or only the spaces between them?
items.answer_should_show: Ice: molecules close together in a neat pattern. Steam: the same H2O molecules far apart. Each molecule stays whole.

items.question: Hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, is used to clean cuts. It has two hydrogens and two oxygens. Draw it so every atom uses all its hands, and no hydrogen holds two partners.
items.answer_should_show: H, O, O, H in a chain: each hydrogen holds one oxygen, and the two oxygens hold each other.

items.question: Design a test to show that the bubbles in the water-splitting test are not steam. Draw what you would do and what you would expect to see.
items.answer_should_show: For example, put a thermometer in the water or feel the glass: it stays cool. Or put an ice cube in the water: the bubbles keep coming.

items.question: Draw a zoomed-in circle of gold, with dots for its atoms. Use one colour or more?
items.answer_should_show: A circle full of dots, all the same colour.

items.question: Sugar is carbon, hydrogen and oxygen joined. Draw a zoomed-in circle of sugar. Use a different colour for each kind of atom.
items.answer_should_show: Dots of three colours, joined in small groups.

items.question: Draw the dark silver before and after the foil bowl. Then draw where the sulfur went.
items.answer_should_show: A dark anklet, a shiny anklet, and the sulfur shown on the foil or in the water.

items.question: Draw what you think the glue's long molecules look like before borax is added, and after. Use dots for the ties.
items.answer_should_show: Before: loose wavy lines. After: wavy lines joined to each other by dots at several places.

items.question: Draw a rubber band's chains when the band is resting, and when it is stretched.
items.answer_should_show: Resting: coiled, wavy chains. Stretched: the same chains pulled straighter and pointing the same way.

items.question: Design a new slime and draw a zoom-in of its chains and ties. Label what you changed and what you expect it to do.
items.answer_should_show: Any clear design, such as more ties for a bouncier slime, with chains and ties drawn and a prediction written.

items.question: Draw a close-up of a sheet of newspaper showing its fibres. Add an arrow along the direction it tears straight.
items.answer_should_show: Many short lines, mostly lying in one direction, and an arrow pointing the same way.

items.question: Draw two pairs of chains. In one pair, the chains are pressed tight together. In the other, small dots sit between the chains. Label which pair is a stiff film and which is a bendy film.
items.answer_should_show: Tight chains labelled stiff. Chains with dots between them labelled bendy.

items.question: Draw a close-up of a cotton yarn: four short fibres overlapping, with the twist drawn as a spiral. Mark where one fibre ends and the next begins.
items.answer_should_show: Four short fibres overlapping along a spiral, with the end points marked.

items.question: Draw the three cups from the potato test after 2 minutes: nothing, raw potato and boiled potato. Show the foam in each.
items.answer_should_show: Tall foam over the raw potato, little or no foam over the boiled potato, and a clear cup with nothing.

items.question: Draw particles in a cold cup and in a warm cup. Show how fast they move and how often they bump.
items.answer_should_show: Few, slow arrows in the cold cup. Many, long arrows and many bumps in the warm cup.

items.question: Draw the Catalyst Tag game: two particles joining with the help of the catalyst, then the catalyst free again.
items.answer_should_show: Three panels: catalyst holding two particles' hands, the pair joined, the catalyst walking away alone.

items.question: Draw a picture that shows why a fine flour dust can burn in a flash but a heap of flour cannot.
items.answer_should_show: Dust spread out in the air, with air around every grain, next to a heap where only the top grains touch the air.

items.question: Invent a catalyst game of your own for a friend. Draw how it shows that the helper is not used up.
items.answer_should_show: Any clear game drawing in which a helper player helps others join or change and stays free at the end.

items.question: Draw two glasses of water side by side, one cold and one warm. Draw dots for particles and arrows to show how fast they move.
items.answer_should_show: Two glasses with dots in each. Short arrows on the dots in the cold glass and long arrows on the dots in the warm glass.

items.question: Draw a mountain with a high path over the top and a low tunnel through it. Label the high path 'no catalyst' and the tunnel 'with catalyst', and draw walkers coming out the other end.
items.answer_should_show: A mountain with a path over the top and a tunnel through it. Labels on each. Walkers coming out at the far end of both.

items.question: Draw one graph with two curves for gas made against time: one for fruit salt in warm water and one in cold water. Label which is which.
items.answer_should_show: Two curves that rise and flatten at the same final height, the warm one rising steeply and flattening sooner, the cold one rising gently and flattening later.

items.question: Draw the two leaves you traced in the leaf test. Circle one place where they are different.
items.answer_should_show: Two leaf outlines, with a circle round a difference such as the tip, the size or a spot.

items.question: Draw yourself in a group with two other animals. Draw the feature you all share at the top.
items.answer_should_show: The child and two animals who share a feature, for example two legs with a crow and a hen, and that feature drawn at the top.

items.question: Draw your ant test: the paper, the three foods, and dots for the ants on each food.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing of the banana, the rice and the insect, with dots showing where the ants gathered.

items.question: Draw two overlapping hoops. One is 'has feathers' and one is 'eats both'. Draw a crow, a parrot and yourself in the right places.
items.answer_should_show: The crow in the middle, the parrot only in 'has feathers', and the child only in 'eats both'.

items.question: Draw two overlapping circles. Label one 'can fly' and one 'has hair'. Put a crow, a cat and a bat in the right places.
items.answer_should_show: Crow in 'can fly' only, cat in 'has hair' only, bat in the middle.

items.question: A mushroom is closer to you than to a tulsi plant. Name one way you and a mushroom are alike that a tulsi plant is not.
items.answer_should_show: Neither of us can make food from sunlight. We both get food from other living things.

items.question: Draw your arm and a bat's wing side by side. Colour the bones that match in the same colour.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing of an arm and a wing, each with one upper bone, two lower bones and finger bones, matching bones in matching colours.

items.question: Draw a family tree with a rohu, a frog, a crow and a cat. Show where each branch splits off.
items.answer_should_show: A tree with a trunk for the backbone, with the rohu on the lowest branch, then the frog, then the crow and the cat on a branch of sealed eggs, with the cat on a final branch for hair and milk.

items.question: Draw a shark, a dolphin and a penguin with the same smooth shape. Under each, write one clue that shows her real group.
items.answer_should_show: Three similar shapes labelled with gills (shark), lungs and milk (dolphin), and feathers (penguin).

items.question: Draw one helper who comes to your building, with the tool they use. Write their name and what they do.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing of a real helper with their tool, their name and their work.

items.question: Draw a line graph of your Shared Pond Test. Put the rounds along the bottom and the fish in the pond up the side. Draw one line for each game.
items.answer_should_show: Two lines: the silent game falling to 0, and the talking game staying near 20.

items.question: Draw your building or street as a pond. Draw the shared things in it, such as the tank, the lift and the park, and the people who use them. Add one rule for each.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing of the building with its shared things, the people who use them and one rule for each.

items.question: Draw two bowls of turmeric water: one after you add lemon juice, one after you add soapy water. Colour them and label each one acid or base.
items.answer_should_show: A yellow bowl labelled 'lemon: acid', and a red-brown bowl labelled 'soap: base'.

items.question: Draw the secret greeting from the challenge: the paper before, and after the turmeric water. Add arrows to show where the base is.
items.answer_should_show: Before: a plain white page with faint marks. After: a yellow page with red letters, and arrows pointing to the letters labelled 'baking soda, a base'.

items.question: Draw a road sign that warns drivers that a school is ahead. Colour its border.
items.answer_should_show: A triangle with a red border, a white middle, and two children drawn in black.

items.question: Draw a map of a road crossing near a school. Put a zebra crossing, a 'School ahead' sign and a traffic light where they should go.
items.answer_should_show: A crossroads with zebra stripes at the crossing near the school gate, a red-bordered triangle with children placed before the school on each side, and a traffic light at the junction.

items.question: Draw the curved Earth with two radio towers far apart. Show how a radio wave can travel from one to the other by bouncing off the ionosphere.
items.answer_should_show: A curved Earth, a layer above it marked ionosphere, and a zigzag line from one tower up to the layer, down to the ground, and up and down again to the far tower.

items.question: Draw the Sun on one side and the Earth on the other. Shade the night half of the Earth. Draw a small person on the day half.
items.answer_should_show: The half of the Earth facing the Sun is left bright, with the person on it. The far half is shaded dark.

items.question: Draw the Earth from above the North Pole as a circle. Draw an arrow showing which way it spins. Draw the Sun on the left. Mark where it is sunrise.
items.answer_should_show: The arrow goes anticlockwise. The Sun is on the left. Sunrise is on the edge where places are just turning from the dark side into the light.

items.question: Draw what the night sky looks like in a 2-hour photo pointed at the Pole Star.
items.answer_should_show: Short curved streaks, like parts of circles, all centred on one bright point near the middle, which is the Pole Star.

items.question: Draw the Earth from above the North Pole with the Sun on one side. Shade the night half. Mark where it is sunrise, and draw an arrow for the way the Earth turns.
items.answer_should_show: A circle for the Earth with the Sun to one side, the far half shaded, an anticlockwise arrow, and sunrise marked on the line between night and day on the side where the Earth is turning into the light.

items.question: Draw a globe with a circle at the equator and a circle at 60 degrees north. Draw arrows to show which place is carried faster, and write how many times faster.
items.answer_should_show: A globe with two circles, a long one at the equator and a half-length one near the top, longer arrow on the equator, and the label 2 times faster.

items.question: Draw the Earth and the Moon. Use arrows to show how the Moon's pull on the tides slows the Earth's spin.
items.answer_should_show: The Earth with a bulge of ocean towards the Moon, an arrow for the Earth's spin, and an arrow showing the tide dragging against the spin. The Moon is drawn a little further away.

items.question: Draw a bean plant at noon and the same plant at 9 at night. Label the leaves 'flat' or 'hanging down'.
items.answer_should_show: Two drawings: at noon the two leaves held out flat, at night the leaves hanging down close to the stem.

items.question: Draw a circle for one year. Mark when barn swallows are in India and when they are in the north. Add what they do in each place.
items.answer_should_show: A circle with the cold months, about October to March, labelled 'India: feeding', and the warm months labelled 'North: nesting and raising chicks', with arrows for the journeys between.

items.question: Draw a graph of how warm your body is across one day, from waking to bedtime. Use your own results if you did the warm and cool test.
items.answer_should_show: A line that starts lowest at waking, rises through the day to the highest point in the late afternoon or early evening, and falls a little by bedtime.

items.question: Design a fair test to find out whether malli buds need warmth to open on time. Draw the setup and label what stays the same.
items.answer_should_show: Two groups of buds from one string, both in the dark, one in a cool place such as near a window at night and one in a warmer place. Same number of buds, same damp cloth, same times for counting.

items.question: Draw yourself dressed for a hot summer afternoon. Colour your clothes.
items.answer_should_show: A child in loose, light-coloured clothes, maybe with a cap and a water bottle.

items.question: Draw a frog by a puddle in the monsoon. Draw what the frog is doing.
items.answer_should_show: A frog by a puddle, with a puffed throat, croaking.

items.question: Draw how a roof could keep a house cooler in summer. Label your idea.
items.answer_should_show: A house with a white roof, with sun rays bouncing off it.

items.question: Draw a tree in the rainy season and the same tree in the dry season. Label what is different.
items.answer_should_show: Two drawings: one tree full of green leaves with wet ground, one with yellow leaves falling or bare branches and dry ground. Labels such as 'green leaves', 'yellow leaves falling', 'dry soil'.

items.question: Draw the Sun at noon in May and at noon in December, over the same house. Draw the shadow of the house for each.
items.answer_should_show: In May, the Sun is high, nearly overhead, and the shadow is very short. In December, the Sun is lower in the south, and the shadow is longer, pointing north.

items.question: Draw a picture that explains why a deciduous tree drops her leaves in the dry season. Show the soil, the roots, the leaves and the water.
items.answer_should_show: Dry soil with little water near the roots, and many leaves losing water through tiny holes, with arrows showing water leaving. A second picture of the bare tree losing much less water.

items.question: Draw a year in the life of a pintail duck. Show where she is in summer, in autumn, in winter and in spring, and why.
items.answer_should_show: Summer: on a lake in Central Asia, laying eggs. Autumn: flying south to India as the lakes freeze. Winter: on a warm Indian lake, feeding. Spring: flying back north to lay eggs.

items.question: Draw a lamp as the Sun and a tilted ball as the Earth. Show India in June and in December, and label which time of year leans towards the Sun and which leans away.
items.answer_should_show: Two drawings with the ball tilted the same way both times. In June, India's half leans towards the Sun. In December it leans away.

items.question: Draw yourself standing in the sunshine at noon. Draw your shadow too.
items.answer_should_show: A child with a small dark shadow close round the feet, and the Sun high above.

items.question: Draw a tree and the tree's shadow in the morning. Then draw the same tree and the shadow in the evening. Draw the Sun each time.
items.answer_should_show: Two trees: in one, the Sun is low on one side and the long shadow points the other way. In the other, the Sun and shadow have swapped sides.

items.question: Design a shade for a bench on a terrace that keeps it shady in the morning and in the evening, not only at noon. Draw it, with the Sun.
items.answer_should_show: A roof with walls or a screen on the east and west sides, or a very wide roof that comes down low on both sides.

items.question: Draw an earthworm in the soil pulling a leaf into a burrow. Label the burrow and a worm cast on the surface.
items.answer_should_show: A worm in a tunnel under a soil line, a leaf at the burrow mouth, and a small curly heap labelled worm cast on top.

items.question: Draw a mushroom and the part of the fungus hidden in the soil.
items.answer_should_show: A mushroom with a wide web of thin threads, the mycelium, spreading in the soil below.

items.question: Draw the path of a carbon atom from the air to a leaf, to the soil, and back to the air.
items.answer_should_show: A circle of arrows: air to leaf, leaf to soil and decomposers, decomposers to air.

items.question: Draw two pictures of a rotting log. In the first, show which gas goes up into the air. In the second, show which materials go down into the soil.
items.answer_should_show: Log with carbon dioxide arrows going up and water vapour. Log with minerals, humus and nutrients going down to a root.

items.question: Draw a loop for carbon: the air, a leaf, a goat and a fungus. Then draw a straight arrow for energy that starts at the Sun and ends as heat.
items.answer_should_show: A circle for carbon through air, leaf, goat, fungus and back to air. A straight line from the Sun to heat.

items.question: Draw a food web with at least five living things from a pond. Join them with arrows that point to the eater.
items.answer_should_show: For example: algae → mosquito larva, algae → tadpole, mosquito larva → small fish, tadpole → small fish, small fish → kingfisher, tadpole → heron.

items.question: Draw an energy pyramid for grass, deer and tiger. Make each layer the right size.
items.answer_should_show: A wide bottom layer of grass, a smaller middle layer of deer, and a tiny top layer with one tiger.

items.question: Draw this food web from a city balcony: a tulsi plant, aphids (tiny sap-sucking insects), a ladybird, a spider, a house gecko and a crow. Join them with arrows that point to the eater. Then cross out the spider and circle every living thing whose life would change.
items.answer_should_show: Arrows: tulsi → aphids, aphids → ladybird, aphids → spider, spider → gecko, gecko → crow. Without the spider, more aphids survive, so the tulsi loses more sap. The ladybird has more aphids to eat. The gecko loses a food, so the crow may find fewer geckos. Almost everything is circled.

items.question: Draw a food chain of four links starting from a rice field. Put an arrow between each link, a level number under each link, and a small red arrow of heat leaving each one.
items.answer_should_show: Rice plant to grasshopper to frog to snake, with arrows pointing to the eater, levels 1 to 4 beneath, and a red heat arrow from every one.

items.question: A deer carries 3000 ticks. Draw the pyramid of numbers for the grass, the deer and the ticks, and write what is odd about its shape.
items.answer_should_show: A thin bar for the grass or a line, a thin bar for one deer, and a very wide bar for the ticks. The shape is upside down at the top, not a pyramid.

items.question: Draw the dead-leaf chain of a mangrove creek. Label the detritus, one detritivore, one decomposer and one animal who eats them.
items.answer_should_show: A fallen mangrove leaf in the mud labelled detritus. A crab labelled detritivore. Fungus or bacteria on the leaf labelled decomposer. A prawn or fish eating small animals from the mud.

items.question: Draw a bee visiting two flowers. Draw dots for the pollen she carries from the first flower to the second.
items.answer_should_show: A bee at one flower with dots on her body, an arrow to a second flower, and dots left in the second flower.

items.question: Draw a cross-section of a forest floor. Show leaf litter, soil, a root, a worm tunnel and rain sinking in.
items.answer_should_show: A layer of leaves on top, soil below, a root going down, a tunnel for a worm, and arrows showing water going down through the litter and the tunnels.

items.question: Draw the pond in the Shared Pond game over four rounds, when the villagers take too much. Show how the number of fish changes.
items.answer_should_show: Four ponds in a row with fewer and fewer fish, such as 20, 10, 5 and then none, with arrows showing the villagers taking fish and a few new fish being born.

items.question: Draw a web around one tree on your street. Show at least five links and name the kind of each.
items.answer_should_show: A tree in the middle, with at least five arrows to different visitors, such as a bird, an ant, a bee, a squirrel and a termite, each labelled food, shelter, travel, making new plants or clean-up.

items.question: Draw your circuit: a cell, two wires and a bulb. Draw arrows to show the electricity going round.
items.answer_should_show: A cell with one wire from each end to the bulb, and arrows going round in a ring.

items.question: Draw a circuit that looks neat but will not light. Then draw a messy one that will.
items.answer_should_show: A neat drawing with a gap, or with both wires on one end, and a messy drawing with every join in place.

items.question: Draw a circuit where the wire goes all the way round a plate of idli before it reaches the bulb. Will it light?
items.answer_should_show: A circuit with a long wire curving round a plate, with both ends of the cell joined to the bulb. Yes, it lights.

items.question: Draw the prints from your Dry Hands Test. Draw one hand for each way of drying, and colour the wet parts.
items.answer_should_show: Four hands, with wet prints for not dried and shaken, perhaps a few wet fingers for clothes, and no wet parts for the towel.

items.question: Draw your Spill Test from above: the floor, the paper extension board and the puddle. Show how far the water ran.
items.answer_should_show: A floor with a tumbler on its side, a puddle spreading, and the paper board, with the puddle reaching it or nearly reaching it.

items.question: Invent a new safety helper for a socket that a toddler cannot open. Draw it. A grown-up writes your label for how it works.
items.answer_should_show: Any clear design, such as a socket with a cover that opens only with two hands, or a socket placed high up out of reach.

items.question: Draw a cell, a bulb and two wires joined so that the bulb lights. Then draw arrows to show the path of the electricity, all the way round.
items.answer_should_show: A loop: from one end of the cell, along a wire to the bulb's tip, through the bulb, out of its metal side, along the second wire, and back to the other end of the cell. The arrows go round in one direction.

items.question: Draw a circuit with a cell, a bulb and a paper clip switch. Draw it twice: once with the switch open, once with it closed.
items.answer_should_show: Two loops. In the open one, the clip is off one pin, there is a gap, and the bulb is dark. In the closed one, the clip touches both pins and the bulb is lit.

items.question: Design a steady hand game. Draw the foil path, the wand, the cell and the bulb, and mark where the gap is.
items.answer_should_show: A wavy foil path joined to one end of the cell. A wand joined to the bulb, and the bulb joined to the other end of the cell. The gap is between the wand and the path.

items.question: Draw a loop with one cell, one bulb and two paper clip switches, so the bulb lights only when both switches are closed.
items.answer_should_show: One loop with both switches in it, one after the other. If either switch is open, there is a gap, so the bulb is dark. Only when both are closed is the loop complete.

items.question: Draw a circuit diagram of one cell and two bulbs side by side. Use the symbols and mark the plus end of the cell.
items.answer_should_show: A cell with two bulbs on two separate branches between the same two points, drawn with a ruler, with the long line of the cell marked plus.

items.question: Draw a circuit with a cell, a bulb and two switches so that the bulb lights only when both switches are closed. Use the symbols.
items.answer_should_show: A cell, a bulb and two switches all in one loop, one after the other.

items.question: Draw a circuit diagram of a home with a light, a fan and a socket, each on its own branch with its own switch, so that each can be used alone.
items.answer_should_show: Two supply lines with three branches between them: one with a switch and a light, one with a switch and a fan, one with a switch and a socket.

items.question: Draw a balloon over your head, just after you rubbed it on your hair. Put minus signs where the extra electrons are, and plus signs where electrons are missing. Draw arrows to show the pulls and pushes.
items.answer_should_show: Minus signs on the rubbed side of the balloon. Plus signs on the hairs. Arrows from the hairs up towards the balloon, and small arrows between the hairs pointing apart.

items.question: Draw a paper bit just below a rubbed balloon. Inside the paper, draw where the plus and minus charges move. Draw an arrow to show which way the paper moves.
items.answer_should_show: Minus on the balloon. Plus signs crowded on the top of the paper, near the balloon, and minus signs on the bottom. An arrow pointing up.

items.question: Draw a storm cloud. Show where the plus charge gathers, where the minus charge gathers, and a lightning bolt to the ground.
items.answer_should_show: Plus signs at the top of the cloud, minus signs near the bottom, and a bolt from the bottom of the cloud down to the ground.

items.question: Draw the charge detector jar with a rubbed balloon held near its foil ball. Show where the extra electrons go, and what the two foil strips do.
items.answer_should_show: Minus on the balloon. Electrons pushed down the clip into the strips, so both strips have minus signs and spread apart in a V. The foil ball at the top has plus signs.

items.question: Design a poster for your building's lift: 'What to do in a thunderstorm'. Show four rules with a picture for each.
items.answer_should_show: Four clear rules with pictures, for example: go inside at the first thunder, stay off the terrace, no baths or washing up during the storm, wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

items.question: Draw a charge ladder with three rungs: wool at the top, cotton in the middle and polythene at the bottom. Draw arrows showing which way electrons go between each neighbouring pair.
items.answer_should_show: A ladder with wool, cotton and polythene from top to bottom, and arrows pointing down from wool to cotton and from cotton to polythene.

items.question: Draw two balloons hanging from one point after both are rubbed the same way. Show the forces on one balloon with arrows.
items.answer_should_show: Two balloons hanging in a V from one point. On each balloon, an arrow down for its weight, an arrow along the thread, and an arrow pointing sideways away from the other balloon.

items.question: Draw a bumblebee flying towards a flower. Mark the kind of charge on the bee and on the flower, and draw an arrow for the pull on a grain of pollen.
items.answer_should_show: A bee marked plus and a flower marked minus, with an arrow from the pollen grain on the flower towards the bee.

items.question: Draw one appliance in your home that makes movement. Draw an arrow to show what moves.
items.answer_should_show: Any appliance that moves, such as a fan with arrows round the blades or a mixie with an arrow round the blade.

items.question: Draw a phone being charged. Show where its electricity comes from, and where it goes.
items.answer_should_show: A phone with a charger wire going to a wall socket, and an arrow from the socket into the phone.

items.question: Your heart has no plug and no cell. Draw a child, and show where the energy for her heartbeat comes from.
items.answer_should_show: A child with a heart drawn inside, and an arrow from food on a plate to the heart.

items.question: Draw a torch. Show with arrows where the energy starts, where it travels, and what it turns into.
items.answer_should_show: Arrows from the cells, along the wire or metal strip, to the bulb, with light coming out and a little heat.

items.question: Draw an energy chain from the Sun to a lit diya. Draw at least 4 steps, with an arrow between each.
items.answer_should_show: For example: the Sun, a sesame or groundnut plant, oil pressed from the seeds, the diya flame giving light and heat.

items.question: Design a machine that uses falling water to ring a bell. Draw it, and label where the energy starts and every change it goes through.
items.answer_should_show: For example: a bottle of water on a high shelf, a pipe, a small paper wheel turned by the falling water, a string on the wheel that pulls a spoon against a tumbler. Labels: stored energy from height, movement, sound.

items.question: Draw an LED bulb with two arrows, one for the useful energy and one for the spread-out energy. Make the arrows the right sizes.
items.answer_should_show: A bulb with a big arrow labelled light and a smaller arrow labelled warmth.

items.question: Draw two bars: one for a slow climb of 34 watts and one for a fast climb of 102 watts. Label each bar.
items.answer_should_show: Two bars, with the fast bar three times as tall as the slow bar.

items.question: Draw an energy chain for you climbing the stairs, from sunlight to the warmth you give to the air.
items.answer_should_show: Sunlight, then a plant, then the food, then the muscles, then movement and warmth in the air, joined by arrows.

items.question: Draw a tumbler of hot milk with a steel spoon standing in it. Draw red arrows to show where the heat moves.
items.answer_should_show: Arrows from the milk into the spoon, up the spoon handle, and from the handle and the tumbler out into the air.

items.question: Draw a zoomed-in picture of the steel inside a ladle handle, with the hot end on the left and the cool end on the right. Show how the tiny particles move.
items.answer_should_show: Rows of particles staying in place. Those on the left shake hard, and the shaking gets smaller towards the right.

items.question: Draw a graph sketch of the Ladle Line. Put the dot's height (2, 4, 6, 8 cm) along the bottom and the time it fell up the side. Use made-up numbers like the ones you found. Does your line go straight, or curve?
items.answer_should_show: The line curves upward and gets steeper, because each dot took longer than the last.

items.question: Design a cup that keeps tea hot for a long time and is cool to hold. Draw it and label what each part is made of.
items.answer_should_show: For example, a cup with two walls and air between them, a lid, and a wooden or plastic handle.

items.question: Draw a pot of water on a flame. Draw arrows to show a convection current inside it.
items.answer_should_show: A pot over a flame. Arrows go up in the middle, across the top, down at the sides and back along the bottom towards the flame.

items.question: Draw an old house on a hot day. Show where cool air comes in, where hot air goes out, and which way each one moves.
items.answer_should_show: A house with a low door or window open on the shaded side and a high ventilator. Arrows show cool air coming in low and moving along the floor, and hot air rising and leaving through the high ventilator.

items.question: Draw a rooftop solar water heater with a tank on top and a black panel below it. Show where the water goes as it warms.
items.answer_should_show: A black panel at the bottom with water inside, a tank above it. Arrows show warm water rising from the panel into the tank, and cool water sinking from the tank back into the panel.

items.question: Draw one thing in your home that makes warmth, and one thing that keeps warmth in.
items.answer_should_show: For example, the Sun at the window, and a quilt on the bed.

items.question: On a cold morning, a sparrow or a crow puffs up their feathers. Draw how they look, and say why they do it.
items.answer_should_show: A round, fluffy bird. The puffed feathers hold more still air, which keeps their warmth in.

items.question: You hold a cold steel tumbler of fridge water in your hands. Draw an arrow to show which way the heat moves.
items.answer_should_show: An arrow from the hand into the tumbler.

items.question: Draw a tumbler of hot water on a table. Draw red arrows to show where its heat goes.
items.answer_should_show: Red arrows go out of the water into the air above it, out through the sides into the air, and down into the table.

items.question: Draw what the water particles might look like in a tumbler of cold water and in a tumbler of hot water. Show how they move.
items.answer_should_show: Both drawings show many small dots packed close together. The cold ones have short wiggle lines. The hot ones have long wiggle lines, showing they jiggle faster.

items.question: Draw two thermometers. Put one in melting ice and one in water boiling in an open pot at sea level. Write what each one reads.
items.answer_should_show: The first thermometer shows 0 °C, in a glass with ice floating in water. The second shows about 100 °C, in a pot with bubbles and steam.

items.question: Draw a graph of temperature against time for a lump of ice that is warmed steadily until it becomes warm water. Mark the flat part.
items.answer_should_show: The line rises from below zero to 0, then stays flat while the ice melts, then rises again as the water warms.

items.question: Draw two small graphs of temperature through a day and a night. One is for a town by the sea, and one is for a town in the middle of a desert.
items.answer_should_show: The sea town graph is a gentle wave with a small gap between its highest and lowest points. The desert town graph is a steep wave with a big gap, hot by day and cold by night.

items.question: Draw the roll-back jar as if you could see through it. Show the band, the padlock and the twist after 3 turns.
items.answer_should_show: A jar on its side with a band from the middle of the base to the middle of the lid, a padlock hanging from the band's middle, and the band twisted on both sides of the padlock.

items.question: Draw the Pop-Up Jumper folded flat with the band on the outside. Use an arrow to show which way the band pulls.
