items.answer_should_show: The Sun, then Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars in order, with an arrow from the Earth pointing towards the Sun.

items.question: Draw the patch of light in the torch test at 20 cm and at 40 cm, side by side, on squared paper.
items.answer_should_show: A 4 by 4 square at 20 cm and an 8 by 8 square at 40 cm, with the second one shaded lighter.

items.question: Draw what the Earth and the Moon might look like from Mars, through a small telescope. Label which is which.
items.answer_should_show: Two dots side by side, a bigger blue-white one labelled Earth and a smaller grey one labelled Moon, both lit on the same side.

items.question: Draw the young solar system as scientists think it looked: a flat spinning disc round the new Sun. Show where rock planets grew and where giant planets grew, and write why.
items.answer_should_show: A flat disc round the Sun. Small rocky planets close in, where it was too warm for ice. Giant planets further out, where ice could freeze, so they grew bigger and gathered gas.

items.question: Draw a young, hot planet in two pictures. In the first, the iron and the rock are mixed. In the second, the heavy iron has sunk to the middle.
items.answer_should_show: Picture one shows a ball with mixed dots of dark iron and light rock. Picture two shows a dark iron core at the middle with a layer of rock round it.

items.question: Draw sunlight reaching Venus, and the heat from its ground trying to escape. Show what its thick air does to the heat.
items.answer_should_show: Yellow arrows of sunlight come in through a thick layer of air. Orange arrows of heat go up from the ground, but many bounce back down from the air layer, so the ground gets hotter.

items.question: Draw a scale model of the Sun and the Earth side by side, with the sizes and the distance between them.
items.answer_should_show: A disc 14 centimetres wide for the Sun and a dot 1 millimetre wide for the Earth, 15 metres away. A break mark shows the long gap.

items.question: Draw the young solar system with the frost line. Show where rocky planets formed, where giants formed, and explain why in one line.
items.answer_should_show: A Sun at the middle of a flat disc. Small rocky planets inside a dotted frost line, because only rock and metal could be solid there. Large giants outside it, where ice could freeze as well, so there was more to gather.

items.question: Draw the Moon as you saw it from your window. Shade in its dark patches.
items.answer_should_show: The Moon's shape that night, with grey patches shaded in.

items.question: Draw the window, one paper strip on the glass, and the Moon. Then draw where the strip looks to be after you walk to the other slipper. Draw an arrow for the way it slid.
items.answer_should_show: The strip drawn in two places with an arrow between them, and the Moon in the same place both times.

items.question: Draw the Sun, the Moon and you. Draw arrows to show how sunlight travels until you see the Moon.
items.answer_should_show: An arrow from the Sun to the Moon, and an arrow from the Moon to the child's eyes.

items.question: Draw the seven stars of the Saptarishi twice. First, as you see them from Earth. Second, as they would look from the side, at their real distances.
items.answer_should_show: First drawing: a ladle, four stars in a bowl and three in a handle. Second drawing: five stars close together and two, Kratu and Marichi, much further away.

items.question: Draw the night sky above your balcony with three stars of different brightness. Draw the city lights below. Show with arrows how the city light hides the faintest star.
items.answer_should_show: Arrows of light from streetlights going up and lighting the air. The faintest star is lost in that glow, while the brightest still shows.

items.question: Design a model, like the thread model, for Orion. Draw where you would place Betelgeuse (about 550 light-years away) and Bellatrix (about 250 light-years away) on their threads, using 1 centimetre for every 10 light-years.
items.answer_should_show: Betelgeuse's paper star at about 55 centimetres along its thread, and Bellatrix's at about 25 centimetres.

items.question: Draw the stars as you would see them looking north for one hour. Show the Pole Star and three stars at different distances from it, with arcs showing how they move.
items.answer_should_show: The Pole Star stays at the middle. Each of the three other stars draws an arc round it, anticlockwise, all of the same angle, 15 degrees. Stars further from the Pole Star draw longer arcs.

items.question: Draw the Earth with its axis, the direction to the Pole Star, and a person in Chennai with a flat horizon. Mark the angle between the horizon and the Pole Star, and write its size.
items.answer_should_show: A ball with a line through it from pole to pole. A line from Chennai parallel to the axis towards the Pole Star. A flat horizon at Chennai. An angle of 13 degrees between the horizon and the line.

items.question: Draw the sky as seen by someone standing exactly at the North Pole. Show where the Pole Star is, and how the other stars move.
items.answer_should_show: The Pole Star is straight overhead. The other stars circle round it in flat circles, parallel to the ground, and none rises or sets.

items.question: Draw the Sun, the Earth's orbit, and the Earth at two points six months apart. Show a near star shifting against faraway stars as seen from the two points.
items.answer_should_show: The Sun at the middle of an oval ring. The Earth on opposite sides of the ring. A near star with lines to the Earth at each point, and the two lines ending at different spots among the faraway stars.

items.question: Draw yourself on a hot day. Show where the sunshine falls and where the shade is. Colour the place you would sit to stay cool.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with sunshine on one side and shade on the other, and the child sitting in the shade.

items.question: Draw the Sun, the Moon and the Earth. Draw an arrow to show the Sun's light going to the Moon, and another arrow from the Moon to the Earth.
items.answer_should_show: A Sun with an arrow to the Moon, and an arrow from the Moon to the Earth.

items.question: Draw the Sun, the Earth and the Moon. Draw arrows to show where the Moon's light comes from and where it goes.
items.answer_should_show: An arrow from the Sun to the Moon, and another arrow from the Moon to the Earth.

items.question: Draw the Sun with three planets going round it. Then draw one moon going round one of the planets. Label each one.
items.answer_should_show: The Sun in the middle, three planets on round paths around it, and a small moon on a small path round one planet, all labelled.

items.question: Draw a magnifying glass above a sheet of paper in the sun. Draw the lines of sunlight going through the glass and meeting in a tiny dot on the paper.
items.answer_should_show: Straight lines of sunlight coming down, bending as they pass through the glass, and meeting at one point on the paper.

items.question: Draw the Sun cut in half like an orange. Show the core in the middle, a wiggly path for the energy getting out, and a straight arrow from the surface to a small Earth.
items.answer_should_show: A circle with a small centre labelled core, a zigzag line from the core to the edge, and a straight arrow from the edge to a small Earth, labelled 8 minutes.

items.question: Design a poster for your building telling children three safe ways to watch a solar eclipse. Draw each way.
items.answer_should_show: Three clear drawings, such as a colander making little suns on paper, a covered mirror making a Sun picture on a wall, and a child wearing eclipse glasses marked ISO 12312-2, with the words 'Never look at the Sun'.

items.question: Draw the Sun three times. In the first, show a spot just arriving at one edge. In the second, show it in the middle. In the third, show it leaving at the other edge. Draw how its shape changes.
items.answer_should_show: Three circles with a spot. At the edge the spot is thin and squashed. In the middle it is round. At the other edge it is thin again.

items.question: Draw the Sun with its wind. Show three arrows of wind going out, and draw the Earth with a bubble of the Sun's wind round it.
items.answer_should_show: A circle for the Sun, arrows going out in all directions, and the Earth inside a large bubble of wind.

items.question: Draw a timeline of what the Sun sends to the Earth after a big eruption. Mark 8 minutes, 1 day and 4 days.
items.answer_should_show: A line with a flash at 8 minutes, a fast cloud near 1 to 3 days, and ordinary wind at about 4 days.

items.question: Plan a game to test if you can tell how far away a sound is. Draw a chair where you sit with your eyes covered, a near spot and a far spot where a grown-up taps.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing of a chair with one spot close behind it and one spot far away.

items.question: Draw something you can hear right now but cannot see.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing of a sound-maker that is out of sight, such as a bird outside or a cooker in the kitchen.

items.question: Draw an elephant listening to her family far away. Draw her family small, at the other side of the page.
items.answer_should_show: An elephant on one side, with tiny elephants far away on the other side, and maybe lines for the rumble between them.

items.question: Draw the ear from the side, cut open, and label the ear flap, ear canal, eardrum, three tiny bones and cochlea.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with the ear flap outside, a tube going in, a thin skin at its end, three small bones behind it and a snail-shaped coil.

items.question: Draw the band of pitches, from very low to very high. Show where people hear, and put an elephant, a dog and a bat where they belong.
items.answer_should_show: A long strip with people in the middle, the elephant reaching below the people's band, the dog reaching a bit above the people's band, and the bat far above the people's band.

items.question: Draw an audiogram for a grandmother who hears low sounds well but high sounds poorly. Put dots from low pitch on the left to high pitch on the right.
items.answer_should_show: Dots high up on the left, near the normal line, dropping lower towards the right.

items.question: Draw a head seen from above with a clap on the right side. Draw a line from the clap to each ear, and show which line is shorter.
items.answer_should_show: A head with two ears, a clap on the right, a short line to the right ear and a longer line to the left ear.

items.question: Draw an ear trumpet beside an ear, pointing at a sound source. Draw arrows to show sound waves entering the wide mouth.
items.answer_should_show: A cone with a wide opening towards the sound, a narrow end near the ear, and arrows going in at the wide end and along to the narrow end.

items.question: Remember the Big Box, Small Box test. Draw your four boxes on a ladder: the deepest sound at the bottom, the highest at the top. Write the sound word next to each.
items.answer_should_show: The big carton at the bottom with 'dhum', then the shoebox, then the toothpaste box, and the matchbox at the top with 'tik'.

items.question: Draw the rhythm of your full name. Draw one big dot for each clap.
items.answer_should_show: A row of dots, one for each part of the child's name. For example, 'Lak-shmi Raj' has 3 dots.

items.question: Design one instrument that can play a high, a middle and a low sound. Draw it and label which part makes each sound.
items.answer_should_show: For example, three boxes of different sizes taped in a row, labelled low for the biggest and high for the smallest. Or three bottles with different amounts of water.

items.question: Draw a bell in the middle of the page. Draw sound lines going out from the bell. Which ways do they go?
items.answer_should_show: Sound lines going out on every side of the bell: up, down, left and right.

items.question: Draw yourself calling a friend with a paper cone. Draw the sound lines coming out of the cone.
items.answer_should_show: A child speaking into the narrow end of a cone, with most sound lines going out of the wide end towards the friend.

items.question: Draw one thing in your home that makes a loud sound. Then draw one thing that makes a soft sound.
items.answer_should_show: One loud sound source, such as a pressure cooker, a mixie or a doorbell, and one soft sound source, such as a clock, a fan or a whisper.

items.question: Draw yourself tapping a steel dabba twice: once to make a soft sound and once to make a loud sound. Show how your hand moves each time.
items.answer_should_show: Two drawings. For the soft sound, a small, gentle movement and small sound lines. For the loud sound, a big swing and big sound lines.

items.question: Draw a temple bell on one side of your page and an ear on the other side. Between them, draw dots for the air molecules. Show them bunched up in some places and spread out in others. Draw one arrow to show which way the sound travels.
items.answer_should_show: The drawing shows the bell, then bands of crowded dots and spread-out dots between the bell and the ear, and an arrow from the bell towards the ear.

items.question: Draw a tin-can telephone: two tins joined by a long, tight string, with one person talking into one tin and another person listening at the other. Draw arrows to show the path of the vibration, from the talker's mouth to the listener's ear.
items.answer_should_show: Arrows go from the mouth into the first tin, along the string, into the second tin, and out to the listener's ear.

items.question: Draw the air between a drum and an ear twice. In the first drawing, the drum has been hit gently. In the second, it has been hit hard. Use dots for the air molecules, and show how the two drawings are different.
items.answer_should_show: Both drawings have bands of crowded dots and spread-out dots, the same distance apart. In the hard-hit drawing, the crowded bands are much more crowded and the spread-out bands much more spread out.

items.question: Draw two bottles, one with a lot of water and one with a little. Mark the air column in each, and say which gives the higher note when blown across.
items.answer_should_show: A bottle with a lot of water has a short air column marked at the top and gives the higher note. A bottle with a little water has a long air column and gives the lower note.

items.question: Draw a string vibrating as one whole loop, and the same string vibrating in two halves. Mark which one gives the higher note.
items.answer_should_show: The first string has one loop between its ends. The second has two loops, with a still point in the middle. The two-loop string is the higher note, one octave above.

items.question: Draw the vocal tract as a bottle shape, and show where the buzz starts and where the vowel is made.
items.answer_should_show: A bottle shape for the throat and mouth. A zig-zag buzz at the bottom where the vocal folds are, and the mouth shape at the top labelled as where the vowel is made.

items.question: Draw a dupatta with a bump on it. Draw one arrow to show which way the bump travels, and another to show which way a clothes peg on it moves.
items.answer_should_show: The bump arrow points along the dupatta towards the door. The peg arrow points up and down.

items.question: Draw a tray seen from the side, with water in it. Draw a wave travelling across it, and label the crest and the trough.
items.answer_should_show: A side view of a tray with a wavy water surface, the top labelled crest and the bottom labelled trough.

items.question: Draw the Earth cut in half. Show the crust, the mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core. Draw one earthquake wave bending as it goes through.
items.answer_should_show: A circle with layers from outside to inside: crust, mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core, and a curved line through them.

items.question: Draw a tray with ripples from slow taps on one side and ripples from fast taps on the other. Show the difference in the gaps.
items.answer_should_show: Two sets of curved or straight lines, with wide gaps for slow taps and narrow gaps for fast taps. A strong drawing shows about half the gap for double the taps.

items.question: Draw two waves on the same line, both moving at the same speed. Make one with a higher frequency than the other. Show how their wavelengths differ.
items.answer_should_show: Two wavy lines, one with crests close together and one with crests far apart. The one with crests close together has the higher frequency and the shorter wavelength.

items.question: Draw the three slices of carrot you traced: from the thick end, the middle and near the tip.
items.answer_should_show: Three circles that get smaller and smaller.

items.question: Draw what Pulli the flat girl would see as a ball passed slowly down through her flat world. Draw 4 boxes, one after another.
items.answer_should_show: A dot, a small circle, a big circle, a small circle (or a dot).

items.question: Draw a net that would fold up into a dice. Use 6 squares joined at their sides.
items.answer_should_show: Six squares joined edge to edge, for example in a cross shape.

items.question: Draw two of the same tree: one near you, and one far away.
items.answer_should_show: A big tree low on the page and a small tree higher up.

items.question: Draw your three strips from the bottle strip test, side by side, and write how many steps away each was.
items.answer_should_show: Three strips getting shorter: 1 step longest, 2 steps about half, 4 steps shortest.

items.question: Draw what you think is at the edge of space, if there is an edge. Then write one question about your drawing.
items.answer_should_show: Any drawing, with a question such as 'What is past the wall?'

items.question: Draw your salt timer. Draw the cone, the hole, the salt stream and the tumbler.
items.answer_should_show: A cone with a small hole at the bottom, a thin line of salt falling, and a tumbler below.

items.question: Draw the four banana cards the way one person in your family laid them out. Add an arrow to show which way time went.
items.answer_should_show: Four cards in a row, from whole banana to peel, with an arrow from first to last.

items.question: Draw the biggest crystal you grew in the slow glass. Draw it as big as your hand. Label one face and one corner.
items.answer_should_show: A cube or a square-sided block, with a face and a corner labelled.

items.question: Draw what you think the particles look like inside a salt crystal, and inside a glass bangle.
items.answer_should_show: Particles in neat rows and columns for salt. Particles in a jumble for glass.

items.question: Draw a model of a salt crystal growing. Show the particles, and one new particle joining. Then draw where you think it would not fit.
items.answer_should_show: Particles in a square pattern, a new particle fitting into the next place in a row, and a crossed-out particle sitting crooked.

items.question: Draw two glasses. In one, draw salt water. In the other, draw rava in water. Show what you would see.
items.answer_should_show: Salt water drawn clear, with nothing on the bottom. Rava water with grains lying on the bottom and clear water above.

items.question: Draw what you think is happening to a salt grain when it dissolves. Draw the water particles too.
items.answer_should_show: Water particles around the grain, pulling small salt particles off its outside, and salt particles spread among the water particles.

items.question: Draw a bar chart of the Full Glass Test: one bar for salt and one bar for sugar, showing how many spoons dissolved.
items.answer_should_show: A short bar of about 3 for salt and a much taller bar of at least 10 for sugar, with the sugar bar marked 'still going'.

items.question: Draw two glasses of soda just after they are opened. Show a cold soda and a warm soda. Draw the bubbles in each.
items.answer_should_show: The cold soda with a gentle thread of small bubbles. The warm soda with many large bubbles and foam rising over the top.

items.question: Draw a drop of food colour falling into a still glass of water. Draw it at the start, after one minute, and after ten minutes.
items.answer_should_show: A dark drop at the top at the start, a spreading cloud of colour after one minute, and an even pale colour through the whole glass after ten minutes.

items.question: Draw a zoomed-in picture of a soap molecule at the edge of a grease drop in water.
items.answer_should_show: A grease drop in the middle, with tadpole-shaped soap molecules around the drop, tails pointing into the grease and heads pointing out into the water.

items.question: Draw the closed box at the end of the Closed Box Test. Show the cloth, the drops, and arrows for water leaving the cloth and landing back.
items.answer_should_show: A box with a wet cloth at the bottom, drops under the lid, and arrows going up from the cloth and the same number coming back down.

items.question: Draw a cold tumbler of ice water in a room. Draw dots for water vapour particles in the air, and show what happens when they touch the tumbler.
items.answer_should_show: Dots spread out in the air, and near the tumbler some dots joining into drops on its surface.

items.question: Draw a pan of boiling water with a lid on. Show the vapour rising, the drops under the lid, and the drops falling back.
items.answer_should_show: A pan with a lid, arrows of vapour rising from the water, drops on the underside of the lid, and drops falling back into the water.

items.question: Draw how the Sun's heat travels from the sea to a monsoon cloud and out again. Show the vapour, the cloud and the heat.
items.answer_should_show: Sea water evaporating, with arrows of vapour carrying heat upward, a cloud forming where the vapour condenses, and heat arrows going out into the air around the cloud.

items.question: Draw a pressure cooker on a stove. Show where the pressure is high, and say why the water inside gets hotter than 100 degrees.
items.answer_should_show: A closed pot with steam trapped inside, arrows showing pressure pushing on the lid and walls, and a label saying that the high pressure raises the boiling point.

items.question: Draw the bucket from your test. Draw the things that floated at the top, and the things that sank at the bottom.
items.answer_should_show: A bucket with the rolling pin, lemon and other floaters at the top, and the coin, spoon and potato on the bottom.

items.question: Draw a ball being pushed down into water. Draw an arrow to show which way the water pushes.
items.answer_should_show: A ball under water, with hands on top, and an arrow pointing up from under the ball.

items.question: Draw a boat floating on water. Draw one arrow for the boat's weight and one for the upthrust. Make the arrows the right lengths.
items.answer_should_show: A boat on the water, with a downward arrow for weight and an upward arrow for upthrust, both the same length.

items.question: Draw a glass with three layers: oil, water and syrup. Label which layer is on top and which is at the bottom, and write why.
items.answer_should_show: A glass with oil on top, water in the middle and syrup at the bottom, with a short reason such as that oil is the least dense and syrup is the most dense.

items.question: Draw a bottle diver in a bottle. Draw the air bubble in the diver before you squeeze and after you squeeze, and say what happens to the diver.
items.answer_should_show: Two bottles, one with a larger air bubble and the diver near the top, and one with a smaller bubble and the diver sinking, with a note that squeezing squashes the air so the diver pushes aside less water.

items.question: Draw the coin from the side, just before the water spilled. Show how high the water rose above the coin's edge.
items.answer_should_show: A coin with a rounded dome of water rising clearly above its edge.

items.question: Draw a water strider standing on water, seen from the side. Show the dents their feet make in the water's skin.
items.answer_should_show: An insect with long legs, each foot pressing a small curved dip into the surface without breaking through.

items.question: Draw two zoomed-in circles: one of water particles and one of honey. Show why honey flows more slowly.
items.answer_should_show: Water: small particles with space to slide. Honey: big sugar particles held close to water particles, with arrows showing them clinging.

items.question: Draw a tall tank of water, seen from the side. Draw arrows to show the push on the side wall at three depths.
items.answer_should_show: A tank with three arrows pointing outwards at the wall. The arrow near the top is short and the arrow near the bottom is the longest.

items.question: Draw a kettle with water in it. Show the water level in the body and in the spout.
items.answer_should_show: A kettle with the water at the same height in the spout and in the body, shown by a line across both.

items.question: Draw a bottle with three jets from three holes. Show which jet is longest, and label which hole has the deepest water above it.
items.answer_should_show: A bottle with three arcs. The jet from the lowest hole is longest. The lowest hole is labelled as having the deepest water above it.

items.question: Draw two joined syringes with a small piston and a big piston. Show the push on each with arrows.
items.answer_should_show: A small syringe and a big syringe joined by a tube. A short arrow on the small piston and a long arrow on the big piston.

items.question: Draw your square of chocolate before the warm water and after the warm water.
items.answer_should_show: A square with sharp corners, then a flat, runny puddle in a katori.

items.question: Draw a tumbler of water in the freezer after one hour. Colour where the ice has formed.
items.answer_should_show: A thin layer of ice on top and a ring of ice round the sides, with water still in the middle.

items.question: Draw what you think sugar water would look like if you could zoom in very close. Show the water particles and the sugar particles.
items.answer_should_show: Many small circles for water particles, with a few different circles for sugar particles spread out among them.

items.question: Draw a sugar grain as a block of particles. Then draw it again after one minute in water, with some particles pulled off.
items.answer_should_show: The second drawing shows a smaller block, with rounded corners, and loose particles spread among water particles.

items.question: Draw the hanger balance three times: with the sugar packet beside bottle A, with the packet lifted out, and after the sugar dissolved. Show the straw each time.
items.answer_should_show: First drawing: straw at the line. Second: side A higher, straw swung. Third: straw back at the line.

items.question: Draw the particles in steam. Show how far apart they are and add arrows to show how they move.
items.answer_should_show: Small circles far apart, each with a long arrow in a different direction.

items.question: Draw a closed box of gas. Show the particles and arrows that show what makes pressure on one wall.
items.answer_should_show: A box with particles far apart. Arrows show some particles hitting the wall.

items.question: Draw two boxes of gas of the same size. Put half as many particles in the second box. Label which has the lower pressure.
items.answer_should_show: The first box has twice as many particles, the second has half. The second is labelled lower pressure.

items.question: Draw one drop of colour in a cup of water just after it falls in and a minute after it is stirred. Show the colour particles.
items.answer_should_show: First picture: the colour particles are clumped together in one place. Second picture: they are spread out through the whole cup.

items.question: Draw the same water in the tumbler, in the thin bottle and in the wide bowl. Show how high it stood in each one.
items.answer_should_show: The water at the bindi in the tumbler, tall in the thin bottle, and low and flat in the wide bowl.

items.question: Draw the three bags turned upside down: the stone bag, the water bag and the air bag. Show where the stone, the water and the air are.
items.answer_should_show: The stone at the new bottom of its bag, the water at the new bottom of its bag with a flat top, and the air bag still puffed full.

items.question: Draw the box from the experiment, cut in half so we can see inside. Draw an arrow for light going into the hole and bouncing around inside.
items.answer_should_show: A box with a hole in the lid, and an arrow entering the hole and zig-zagging between the walls, getting shorter or fainter at each bounce, without coming back out.

items.question: Draw the Earth going round the Sun. Next to it, draw the Earth going round a black hole of the same mass. What is the same and what is different?
items.answer_should_show: Two drawings with the Earth on the same-sized path. The Sun is big and bright, the black hole is a tiny black dot. The path is the same. The difference is that the second picture is dark.

items.question: Draw what a watcher far away would see as a cloud of hot gas swirls into a black hole.
items.answer_should_show: A black circle in the middle, with a bright ring or swirl of glowing gas round it. The black part has no light at all.

items.question: Draw a spiral galaxy, an elliptical galaxy and an irregular galaxy. Write the name under each one.
items.answer_should_show: The spiral has a bright middle and curling arms. The elliptical is a smooth oval with no arms. The irregular is a patchy cloud with no clear shape.

items.question: Draw the Bindi Balloon twice, small and big. On the big one, draw arrows from one bindi to the others. Make the arrows longer where the bindis moved further.
items.answer_should_show: Short arrows to near bindis and long arrows to far bindis, from any bindi chosen.

items.question: Draw the Milky Way from the side: a thin disc with a bulge in the middle. Mark the Sun. Draw one arrow along the disc and one arrow up out of it.
items.answer_should_show: A thin line with a bulge in the middle, the Sun about halfway along inside the line, an arrow along the line and an arrow pointing up.

items.question: Draw what the pinhole bunch looked like from close up, and from the far end of the room.
items.answer_should_show: Close up: about 15 separate tiny points. From far: one soft, fuzzy patch of light.

items.question: Design a better streetlight for a city that wants its children to see the Milky Way. Draw it and label how it keeps light out of the sky.
items.answer_should_show: Any design that points light downwards, with a cover or shade on top, uses warm, dim light, or switches off late at night.

items.question: Draw an atom the honest way. Put a tiny dot for the nucleus in the middle, and a cloud for the electrons around it. Label both.
items.answer_should_show: A very small dot in the middle labelled nucleus, with a soft, dotty cloud around it labelled electron cloud, thicker near the middle.

items.question: Draw the card from the marble test, seen from above. Draw the battery as a dot. Draw arrows for 6 marbles: 5 going straight through and 1 bouncing back off the battery.
items.answer_should_show: A square with a small dot. Five straight arrows cross it without touching the dot. One arrow hits the dot and turns back.

items.question: Draw a zoom in 6 circles: your hand, your skin, one cell, one molecule, one atom, and the atom's nucleus. Label each circle.
items.answer_should_show: Six circles, each a closer zoom: a hand, skin, a cell, a molecule of joined balls, an atom drawn as a cloud with a dot, and the dot opened to show protons and neutrons.

items.question: Draw two zoomed-in pictures: the inside of jar A, with peels alone, and the inside of jar B, with peels and paper. Show where there is air and where there is water.
items.answer_should_show: Jar A: peels squashed together, water filling the gaps, no air. Jar B: peels with strips of paper between them, small air spaces, the paper darker where it has soaked up water.

items.question: Draw the journey of a mango skin through the world: from the kitchen, to the compost pot, to the air and the soil, and back into a new plant.
items.answer_should_show: A loop: mango skin into the pot; microbes feeding; arrows to the air (carbon dioxide and water) and into compost; compost in a pot; a plant growing; carbon dioxide going into the plant's leaves.

items.question: Draw what you saw in your jars after two weeks: the peel, the paper, the cloth and the milk packet.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing showing the peel dark and soft or partly gone, the paper soft or torn, the cloth stained, and the milk packet unchanged.

items.question: Draw two napkins from the Napkin Press Test: one with a wet mark, and one with no mark. Write what was on each.
items.answer_should_show: One napkin with a grey patch, labelled peel, rice or tea leaves. One clean napkin, labelled onion skin, dry leaf, wrapper or newspaper.

items.question: Draw what happens to a bag of mixed waste, with peels and packets together. Where does it end up?
items.answer_should_show: A bag going to a big heap at a dump, perhaps with crows, flies or smoke.

items.question: Draw two paths for a piece of newspaper: one if it goes in the dry bin, and one if it goes in a mixed bag.
items.answer_should_show: One path from a dry bin to a kabadiwala, a paper mill and new paper. Another from a mixed bag to a dumping ground, where it rots or burns.

items.question: Draw the path of mercury at Minamata: from the factory, to tiny living things, to small fish, to big fish, to a cat or person. Show the mercury growing at each step.
items.answer_should_show: A chain of drawings with arrows, from the factory pipe to tiny living things, small fish, big fish and a cat, with more and more dots of mercury at each step.

items.question: Draw two glasses of the same muddy water 30 minutes after the Phitkari Test started: glass A without phitkari, glass B with phitkari. Show the clear water and the mud.
items.answer_should_show: Glass A is cloudy all the way down. Glass B has clear water above and a brown layer of mud at the bottom.

items.question: Draw a map of your home's used water: from the kitchen sink to where it ends up. Add arrows.
items.answer_should_show: Sink, drain pipe, building drain, city sewer, sewage treatment plant (or a canal in some places), then a river, lake or the sea.

items.question: Design a home system that sends bath water to the toilet flush. Draw it with arrows and labels.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with a bucket or tank catching bath water, a filter or cloth to catch hair, and a pipe or bucket to the toilet, with labels.

items.question: Draw the water cycle with arrows. Label where water evaporates, where it condenses and where it falls as rain.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing that goes all the way round: the Sun warms the sea, arrows show vapour rising (evaporates), a cloud forms high up (condenses), rain falls on hills, and a river carries the water back to the sea.

items.question: Draw a mountain with the sea on one side. Show the wet wind, the clouds, where the rain falls, and the dry side. Label the dry side 'rain shadow'.
items.answer_should_show: The wind blows from the sea up the near slope. Clouds and rain are on the sea side. The far side is dry and labelled rain shadow.

items.question: Draw one flake of poha from the water katori and one from the oil katori. Show which one squashed.
items.answer_should_show: A fat, soft, squashed flake for water. A flat, shiny, hard flake for oil.

items.question: Draw your home. Draw every place where your family uses water.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with the kitchen tap, the bathroom, the drinking pot or filter, and plants or a pet bowl.

items.question: Draw a well and the ground around it. Show where the groundwater is, and how it gets into the well.
items.answer_should_show: The drawing shows water filling the gaps in soil or rock below the ground, with arrows showing it seeping into the well from the sides and the bottom.

items.question: Draw the journey of one water molecule over a very long time. Show at least five places it has been, from space to your glass.
items.answer_should_show: Any drawing with a sensible order, such as: ice in space, an icy comet or rock, the sea, a cloud, rain, a river, groundwater, a tree, a dinosaur, a well, your glass.

items.question: Draw one street in the monsoon two ways: all cement, and with soil, trees and a pond. Use arrows to show where the rain goes in each.
items.answer_should_show: The cement street shows arrows running off into drains and flooding. The street with soil, trees and a pond shows arrows soaking into the ground and into the pond.

items.question: Draw the steel plate after 1 spray, and again just before the first drop ran down.
items.answer_should_show: First picture: many tiny dots. Second picture: fewer, bigger drops, with one starting to run.

items.question: Draw what you think is inside a grey rain cloud, as if you had a magic magnifying glass.
items.answer_should_show: Lots of tiny drops, some joining together, and a few bigger drops falling out of the bottom.

items.question: Draw a comic strip in 3 boxes: one water drop's journey from the sea, into a cloud, and back down as rain.
items.answer_should_show: Box 1: water evaporating from the sea. Box 2: a tiny drop in a cloud, joining others. Box 3: a big raindrop falling.

items.question: Draw the sky you would expect an hour before a thunderstorm. Label the kind of cloud.
items.answer_should_show: A tall cumulonimbus cloud with a dark bottom and a flat, spreading top, labelled.

items.question: Draw a map with a storm over the sea and your city on the coast. Draw where the storm is today, and where you forecast it will be tomorrow.
items.answer_should_show: A storm drawn over the sea, an arrow, and the storm drawn again nearer to or over the city.

items.question: Draw two lines on a graph that start at almost the same point and slowly spread apart. Label one end 'sunny' and the other 'storm'. Write one sentence saying what the drawing shows.
items.answer_should_show: Two lines starting together and spreading apart, with a sentence such as 'Tiny differences at the start grow into big differences later.'

items.question: Draw the paper strip behind the sweater, and behind the raincoat. Show what each strip did.
items.answer_should_show: Behind the sweater, the strip waves or flies. Behind the raincoat, the strip hangs straight down.

items.question: Draw yourself dressed for a hot, sunny day in May.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with a cap or hat and light, loose clothes, maybe in the shade.

items.question: Draw a windy day. Show three things that the wind is moving.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing with three things the wind moves, such as a bending tree, flapping clothes and a flying kite.

items.question: Draw a cloud. Then draw a zoom-in circle next to it, showing what a cloud is made of.
items.answer_should_show: A cloud with a circle full of tiny round water drops.

items.question: Draw a wind vane. Label the arrowhead, the tail and the pin it turns on. Draw an arrow to show the wind coming from the west.
items.answer_should_show: A vane with a small arrowhead, a bigger tail and a pin. The wind arrow comes from the west, and the vane's arrowhead points west, into the wind.

items.question: Draw a line chart for this day in Chennai: 7 am 27 °C, 10 am 31 °C, 1 pm 34 °C, 3 pm 35 °C, 6 pm 31 °C. Circle the warmest time.
items.answer_should_show: A line rising from 27 to a peak of 35 at 3 pm, then falling to 31, with the 3 pm point circled.

items.question: Design your own weather screen from things at home. Draw it, and label how it keeps sunlight out and lets air in.
items.answer_should_show: Any design with a shade that stops all direct sunlight, gaps or slots for air, a light colour, and the thermometer hanging free inside.

items.question: Draw a beach in the afternoon. Draw an arrow for the warm air over the land, and an arrow for the breeze. Label the land and the sea.
items.answer_should_show: Warm air rising over the land, and an arrow along the ground from the sea onto the land.

items.question: Draw a windmill's blades from the front. Draw an arrow to show which way they will turn when the wind blows at them.
items.answer_should_show: Four or more blades, all tilted the same way, with a curved arrow going round.

items.question: Draw the path of the air in a full sea breeze loop: along the ground, up, high in the sky, and down again. Label where it is warm and where it is cool.
items.answer_should_show: A loop: low from sea to land, up over the warm land, back out over the sea high up, and down over the cool sea.

items.question: Draw four small pictures to show a cell dividing in order. Write one word under each picture.
items.answer_should_show: A round cell with threads in a nucleus, then a cell with X-shaped chromosomes lined up in the middle, then the chromosomes pulled to the two ends, then two separate cells. Words such as copy, line up, pull, split.

items.question: Draw a plant cell and an animal cell, each at the end of division. Show how they finish differently.
items.answer_should_show: An animal cell pinched into two with a narrowing waist, and a plant cell with a new wall across the middle.

items.question: Draw a timeline from a fertilised egg to a child. Mark where cells divide and where they take on different jobs.
items.answer_should_show: A timeline starting with one cell, then 2, 4 and 8 cells, then a ball of cells, then shapes for skin, muscle and nerve cells, ending with a child. Arrows or labels mark division and different jobs.

items.question: Draw a group of onion cells as you saw them. Label one cell, one wall and one nucleus.
items.answer_should_show: Long boxes fitted side by side like bricks, each with a thin outline (the wall) and a dark dot (the nucleus).

items.question: Draw a bacterium finding food by run and tumble. Use straight arrows for the runs and little spirals for the tumbles.
items.answer_should_show: Straight arrows that keep going when they head towards the food, and spirals followed by new arrows when they turn away, ending at the food.

items.question: Draw a plant cell. Label the wall, the membrane, the nucleus, a chloroplast and the big vacuole.
items.answer_should_show: A box-shaped cell with a thick wall outside a thin membrane, a round nucleus, several small green ovals and one large vacuole filling most of the space.

items.question: Draw an amoeba eating a smaller cell. Show the food and how the amoeba takes it in.
items.answer_should_show: A blob-shaped cell with two arms pushed out, curling round a small cell, and a bubble forming round the food inside her.

items.question: Draw two potato cells side by side, one in plain water and one in strong salt water. Draw arrows to show which way the water moves.
items.answer_should_show: A full, round cell in plain water with arrows pointing in, and a shrunken cell in salt water with arrows pointing out.

items.question: Draw the three plates from the sleeping seeds experiment as they looked on the last day, before you watered plate 3. Label the plate that shows water alone does not make things grow.
items.answer_should_show: Plate 1: seeds with long white roots. Plate 2: pebbles on wet cotton, just the same as on day 1, labelled 'water alone does not make things grow'. Plate 3: dry seeds on dry cotton, unchanged.

items.question: Draw a virus outside a cell, and the same virus inside a cell. Under each drawing, write what the virus can do there.
items.answer_should_show: Outside: a virus drifting on their own, labelled 'does nothing, makes no copies'. Inside: a cell full of new viruses, labelled 'the cell reads the virus's instructions and builds copies'.

items.question: Draw a dry karamani seed cut open. Label the baby plant, the food store and the tough coat. Then write which part wakes up first when water arrives, and what it does.
items.answer_should_show: The drawing shows a tough coat, a curled baby plant and a food store. The baby plant wakes first: the cells take in water, use the stored food and send out a root.

items.question: Draw a cell with six rooms. Label each room and write its job in three words.
items.answer_should_show: A cell with a membrane, a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, a Golgi body and a lysosome, each labelled with a short job.

items.question: Draw a mitochondrion with its two skins and the folds. Mark where food and oxygen go in and what comes out.
items.answer_should_show: A bean shape with a double outline and a wavy inner wall. Arrows in for sugar and oxygen, and arrows out for ATP, carbon dioxide and water.

items.question: Draw yourself breathing out on a cold steel plate. Draw what you saw on the plate.
items.answer_should_show: A child and a plate with a cloudy patch on it.

items.question: Draw one living thing you can see from your window.
items.answer_should_show: Any living thing: a crow, a pigeon, a tree, a plant, a dog or a person.

items.question: Draw a baby animal and the grown-up animal they will become.
items.answer_should_show: Any pair, such as a chick and a hen, or a caterpillar and a butterfly.

items.question: Draw the mint in water before and after one hour.
items.answer_should_show: A droopy mint sprig in the first picture, and the same sprig standing up in the second.

items.question: Draw round your hand. Then draw what you think your hand will look like when you are grown up.
items.answer_should_show: A hand outline, and a bigger hand drawn round it.

items.question: Draw the two dabbas from the chuna water test, after three hours. Colour the chuna water that went milky.
items.answer_should_show: Two dabbas, each with a small glass. The glass in the sprout dabba is coloured white. The glass in the empty dabba is clear.

items.question: Draw a plant that senses light. Show where the light comes from and which way the plant bends.
items.answer_should_show: A plant with shoots or leaves bending towards a window or a lamp.

items.question: Plan a test to find out if a whole coconut is alive. Draw what you would do.
items.answer_should_show: A whole coconut with the husk, half buried in damp soil in a big pot, with a note to check for a green shoot every week.

items.question: Draw yourself doing three of the seven signs of life. Label each sign.
items.answer_should_show: For example: eating a dosa, labelled nutrition. Jumping, labelled movement. Pulling a hand away from a hot tawa, labelled sensing.

items.question: Draw two beetroot cells side by side. Draw the first before heating and the second after heating. Show where the red colour is in each one.
items.answer_should_show: The first cell has a whole skin with red dots inside it. The second cell has a broken skin, with red dots leaking out into the water around it.

items.question: Draw a line graph with time across the bottom and temperature up the side. Draw one line for warm water in an open tumbler over 30 minutes. Draw one line for a child's temperature.
items.answer_should_show: The tumbler line slopes downwards towards the room's temperature. The child's line stays almost level.

items.question: Draw a salt crystal growing, and a bean sprout growing, side by side. Use arrows to show what each one takes in and what it becomes.
items.answer_should_show: The crystal has arrows from salt in the water into new cubes on the outside. The sprout has arrows from water, air and food into new roots and leaves, which are different from what went in.

items.question: Draw yourself in the still round of the sound test. Draw three sounds you noticed around you.
items.answer_should_show: A child sitting still with eyes shut, and three sound makers such as a fan, a crow and a car.

items.question: Draw an ant on the kitchen floor. Draw arrows to three things you think the ant notices.
items.answer_should_show: An ant with arrows to things such as a crumb, a drop of water and another ant.

items.question: Draw yourself outside the closed door, listening. Draw what was really making one of the sounds on the other side.
items.answer_should_show: A child by a closed door, and on the other side either a tumbler and spoon, or a phone playing a recording.

items.question: Draw what you think is inside a blown-up balloon, as if your eyes could see tiny things.
items.answer_should_show: A balloon full of tiny dots or balls with space between them, moving about.

items.question: Draw a dream sign: something that could only happen in a dream. Then draw how you would check it.
items.answer_should_show: A drawing of something impossible, such as a fridge full of stars, and a check, such as looking again or asking someone.
